documents.title: The effect of sample site and collection procedure on identification of SARS-CoV-2 infection.
documents.abstract:
BACKGROUND: Sample collection is a key driver of accuracy in the diagnosis of SARS-CoV-2 infection. Viral load may vary at different anatomical sampling sites and accuracy may be compromised by difficulties obtaining specimens and the expertise of the person taking the sample. It is important to optimise sampling accuracy within cost, safety and accessibility constraints.
OBJECTIVES: To compare the sensitivity of different sampling collection sites and methods for the detection of current SARS-CoV-2 infection with any molecular or antigen-based test.
SEARCH METHODS: Electronic searches of the Cochrane COVID-19 Study Register and the COVID-19 Living Evidence Database from the University of Bern (which includes daily updates from PubMed and Embase and preprints from medRxiv and bioRxiv) were undertaken on 22 February 2022. We included independent evaluations from national reference laboratories, FIND and the Diagnostics Global Health website. We did not apply language restrictions.
SELECTION CRITERIA: We included studies of symptomatic or asymptomatic people with suspected SARS-CoV-2 infection undergoing testing. We included studies of any design that compared results from different sample types (anatomical location, operator, collection device) collected from the same participant within a 24-hour period.
DATA COLLECTION AND ANALYSIS: Within a sample pair, we defined a reference sample and an index sample collected from the same participant within the same clinical encounter (within 24 hours). Where the sample comparison was different anatomical sites, the reference standard was defined as a nasopharyngeal or combined naso/oropharyngeal sample collected into the same sample container and the index sample as the alternative anatomical site. Where the sample comparison was concerned with differences in the sample collection method from the same site, we defined the reference sample as that closest to standard practice for that sample type. Where the sample pair comparison was concerned with differences in personnel collecting the sample, the more skilled or experienced operator was considered the reference sample. Two review authors independently assessed the risk of bias and applicability concerns using the QUADAS-2 and QUADAS-C checklists, tailored to this review. We present estimates of the difference in the sensitivity (reference sample (%) minus index sample sensitivity (%)) in a pair and as an average across studies for each index sampling method using forest plots and tables. We examined heterogeneity between studies according to population (age, symptom status) and index sample (time post-symptom onset, operator expertise, use of transport medium) characteristics.
MAIN RESULTS: This review includes 106 studies reporting 154 evaluations and 60,523 sample pair comparisons, of which 11,045 had SARS-CoV-2 infection. Ninety evaluations were of saliva samples, 37 nasal, seven oropharyngeal, six gargle, six oral and four combined nasal/oropharyngeal samples. Four evaluations were of the effect of operator expertise on the accuracy of three different sample types. The majority of included evaluations (146) used molecular tests, of which 140 used RT-PCR (reverse transcription polymerase chain reaction). Eight evaluations were of nasal samples used with Ag-RDTs (rapid antigen tests). The majority of studies were conducted in Europe (35/106, 33%) or the USA (27%) and conducted in dedicated COVID-19 testing clinics or in ambulatory hospital settings (53%). Targeted screening or contact tracing accounted for only 4% of evaluations. Where reported, the majority of evaluations were of adults (91/154, 59%), 28 (18%) were in mixed populations with only seven (4%) in children. The median prevalence of confirmed SARS-CoV-2 was 23% (interquartile (IQR) 13%-40%). Risk of bias and applicability assessment were hampered by poor reporting in 77% and 65% of included studies, respectively. Risk of bias was low across all domains in only 3% of evaluations due to inappropriate inclusion or exclusion criteria, unclear recruitment, lack of blinding, nonrandomised sampling order or differences in testing kit within a sample pair. Sixty-eight percent of evaluation cohorts were judged as being at high or unclear applicability concern either due to inflation of the prevalence of SARS-CoV-2 infection in study populations by selectively including individuals with confirmed PCR-positive samples or because there was insufficient detail to allow replication of sample collection. When used with RT-PCR • There was no evidence of a difference in sensitivity between gargle and nasopharyngeal samples (on average -1 percentage points, 95% CI -5 to +2, based on 6 evaluations, 2138 sample pairs, of which 389 had SARS-CoV-2). • There was no evidence of a difference in sensitivity between saliva collection from the deep throat and nasopharyngeal samples (on average +10 percentage points, 95% CI -1 to +21, based on 2192 sample pairs, of which 730 had SARS-CoV-2). • There was evidence that saliva collection using spitting, drooling or salivating was on average -12 percentage points less sensitive (95% CI -16 to -8, based on 27,253 sample pairs, of which 4636 had SARS-CoV-2) compared to nasopharyngeal samples. We did not find any evidence of a difference in the sensitivity of saliva collected using spitting, drooling or salivating (sensitivity difference: range from -13 percentage points (spit) to -21 percentage points (salivate)). • Nasal samples (anterior and mid-turbinate collection combined) were, on average, 12 percentage points less sensitive compared to nasopharyngeal samples (95% CI -17 to -7), based on 9291 sample pairs, of which 1485 had SARS-CoV-2. We did not find any evidence of a difference in sensitivity between nasal samples collected from the mid-turbinates (3942 sample pairs) or from the anterior nares (8272 sample pairs). • There was evidence that oropharyngeal samples were, on average, 17 percentage points less sensitive than nasopharyngeal samples (95% CI -29 to -5), based on seven evaluations, 2522 sample pairs, of which 511 had SARS-CoV-2. A much smaller volume of evidence was available for combined nasal/oropharyngeal samples and oral samples. Age, symptom status and use of transport media do not appear to affect the sensitivity of saliva samples and nasal samples. When used with Ag-RDTs • There was no evidence of a difference in sensitivity between nasal samples compared to nasopharyngeal samples (sensitivity, on average, 0 percentage points -0.2 to +0.2, based on 3688 sample pairs, of which 535 had SARS-CoV-2).
AUTHORS' CONCLUSIONS: When used with RT-PCR, there is no evidence for a difference in sensitivity of self-collected gargle or deep-throat saliva samples compared to nasopharyngeal samples collected by healthcare workers when used with RT-PCR. Use of these alternative, self-collected sample types has the potential to reduce cost and discomfort and improve the safety of sampling by reducing risk of transmission from aerosol spread which occurs as a result of coughing and gagging during the nasopharyngeal or oropharyngeal sample collection procedure. This may, in turn, improve access to and uptake of testing. Other types of saliva, nasal, oral and oropharyngeal samples are, on average, less sensitive compared to healthcare worker-collected nasopharyngeal samples, and it is unlikely that sensitivities of this magnitude would be acceptable for confirmation of SARS-CoV-2 infection with RT-PCR. When used with Ag-RDTs, there is no evidence of a difference in sensitivity between nasal samples and healthcare worker-collected nasopharyngeal samples for detecting SARS-CoV-2. The implications of this for self-testing are unclear as evaluations did not report whether nasal samples were self-collected or collected by healthcare workers. Further research is needed in asymptomatic individuals, children and in Ag-RDTs, and to investigate the effect of operator expertise on accuracy. Quality assessment of the evidence base underpinning these conclusions was restricted by poor reporting. There is a need for further high-quality studies, adhering to reporting standards for test accuracy studies.

Plain language summary How accurate are different types of sample collection for diagnosing COVID‐19 infection? Key messages • When used with RT‐PCR tests (a molecular test that detects genetic material in COVID‐19 using a technique called reverse transcription polymerase chain reaction), self‐collected gargle and deep throat saliva samples have a similar sensitivity compared to trained healthcare worker‐collected nasopharyngeal samples (taken from the back of the throat through the nose) in detecting COVID‐19. • When used with RT‐PCR, samples collected from the nose, oropharynx (throat via the mouth), oral cavity, and other saliva collection methods are less sensitive for detecting COVID‐19 compared to healthcare worker‐collected nasopharyngeal samples. • When used with rapid antigen tests (Ag‐RDTs; at‐home/self‐tests), samples collected from the nose have a similar sensitivity to healthcare worker‐collected nasopharyngeal samples in detecting COVID‐19. Why is improving the diagnosis of COVID‐19 important? Coronavirus disease (COVID‐19) is caused by infection with severe acute respiratory syndrome coronavirus 2 (SARS‐CoV‐2). People with suspected COVID‐19 may decide to take a test to know whether they are infected, so that they can receive treatment, and follow recommended guidance to self‐isolate and inform close contacts. Not detecting COVID‐19 when it is present (a false negative result) risks spreading infection and results in missed opportunities for treatment. Types of sample collection methods for diagnosing COVID‐19? The type and quality of sample taken for confirmation of COVID‐19 affects the reliability of diagnosis. The most accurate type of sample to diagnose COVID‐19 is that taken by a trained healthcare worker from the back of the throat through the nose (a nasopharyngeal sample). This type of test detects genetic material in the virus using a technique called reverse transcription polymerase chain reaction (RT‐PCR). However, this sample is difficult to obtain correctly, causes discomfort and risks spreading infection if individuals cough or sneeze when the sample is taken. Alternative sample types, particularly those that can be self‐collected using rapid antigen tests (Ag‐RDTs; i.e. self‐tests), may reduce cost and discomfort and improve the safety of sampling. This may, in turn, improve access to and uptake of testing. What did we want to find out? We wanted to compare the sensitivity of different sample sites and collection methods in detecting COVID‐19 with molecular tests (RT‐PCR tests) or self‐based tests (Ag‐RDT tests). What did we do? We searched for studies that had compared the accuracy of nasopharyngeal samples to any alternative that could be used in patients outside of hospital, including nose (nasal) samples, throat samples taken through the mouth (oropharyngeal), gargle samples and saliva samples. We looked at the use of samples with either RT‐PCR or Ag‐RDTs. We also searched for studies that had compared different methods for taking samples, such as samples collected by a healthcare worker compared to those collected by individuals with no or minimal instructions. What did we find? The review included 106 studies with a total of 60,523 participants, of whom 11,045 had COVID‐19 infection. Fifty‐nine per cent of studies were conducted on adults and 79% on symptomatic or mixed symptomatic and asymptomatic participants. Sixty per cent of studies took place in Europe or the USA; just over half (55%) took place in dedicated COVID‐19 testing centres or in outpatient settings. Main results With RT‐PCR, on average: ‐ 100% of positive nasopharyngeal samples collected by healthcare workers would also test positive on self‐collected gargle samples or saliva samples (collected by coughing and then spitting (deep throat saliva)); ‐ 88% of positive nasopharyngeal samples collected by healthcare workers would also test positive with self‐ or healthcare worker‐collected nose samples; ‐ 87% of positive nasopharyngeal samples collected by healthcare workers would also be detected by saliva self‐collected using spitting, 84% by saliva self‐collected using drooling and 79% by saliva self‐collected by sucking on a swab; and ‐ 83% of positive nasopharyngeal samples collected by healthcare workers would also be detected by self‐ or healthcare worker‐collected oropharyngeal samples. With Ag‐RDTs, on average: ‐ 100% of positive nasopharyngeal samples collected by healthcare workers would also be detected by self‐collected or healthcare worker‐collected nose samples. Summary results The results of these studies indicate that in a group of 1000 people, of whom 230 (23%) have COVID‐19, then: when used with PCR, compared to healthcare worker‐collected nasopharyngeal samples: ‐ no cases of COVID‐19 would be missed using self‐collected gargle samples (12 less to 5 more) or deep throat saliva samples (2 less to 48 more); ‐ 28 (16 to 39) fewer cases of COVID‐19 infection would be detected using healthcare worker‐ or self‐collected nose sample; ‐ 30 (18 to 41) fewer cases of COVID‐19 infection would be detected by saliva self‐collected using spitting, 37 (12 to 62) fewer by saliva collected by drooling and 48 (12 to 85) fewer by saliva collected by sucking on a swab; ‐ 39 (12 to 67) fewer cases of COVID‐19 infection would be detected by healthcare worker‐ or self‐collected oropharyngeal samples; and when used with Ag‐RDTs, compared to healthcare worker‐collected nasopharyngeal samples: no cases of COVID‐19 infection would be missed using healthcare worker‐ or self‐collected nose samples. What are the limitations of the evidence? It was often not clear whether included studies deliberately excluded inadequate samples or whether the results of the more accurate nasopharyngeal sample were known when alternative samples were interpreted. This may have resulted in alternative sample types appearing more accurate than they are in practice, decreasing the number of missed cases of COVID‐19 infection. More than half of studies did not give information about how long participants had had symptoms at the time of sampling. This reduces our confidence in the comparison of different sample types. Most studies evaluated self‐collected samples by adults with symptoms for use with RT‐PCR; therefore, the findings of this review may not be applicable to asymptomatic individuals or children. For studies conducted with Ag‐RDTs, it is unclear whether sensitivity estimates of nose samples are applicable to home use (self‐collected and self‐interpreted). How up to date is this review? As of 16 August 2023, there had been 769,774,646 confirmed cases of COVID‐19, including 6.96 million deaths reported to the World Health Organisation (WHO; WHO 2023 ). The majority of confirmed cases have been reported in Europe (2.8 million), followed by the western Pacific (2.1 million) with 1.9 million in the Americas. SARS‐CoV‐2 poses important diagnostic evaluation challenges. These include evaluating whether in vitro diagnostic tests can accurately identify and rule out current SARS‐CoV‐2 infection; whether diagnostic accuracy varies according to participant, test and setting specific factors; and optimisation of diagnostic capability for large‐scale testing programmes. Sample collection is a crucial step in the diagnosis of infectious diseases and a key driver of accuracy ( WHO 2021 ). Viral load is different at different anatomical sampling sites and varies over the course of infection ( Mallett 2020 ; Weiss 2020 ; Wolfel 2020 ). Adequate collection may be compromised by the level of difficulty obtaining specimens, the experience and training of the person taking the sample and discomfort associated with the sampling procedure itself. This review synthesises the evidence for the effect of different anatomical sample collection sites and methods on the accuracy of molecular or antigen tests for the detection of SARS‐CoV‐2. Nasopharyngeal samples are considered to be the most accurate type of sample for detection of SARS‐CoV‐2 ( WHO 2021 ), but adequate samples can be difficult to collect, the procedure is uncomfortable for patients and collection requires the use of personal protective equipment (PPE). Safety concerns, equipment shortages and resource requirements such as the need for training for the purposes of testing on a large scale, have prompted investigation into the accuracy of sampling sites and methods that are safer for patients and healthcare workers and pose fewer logistical and economic barriers to their use. Samples that can be adequately self‐collected reduce the risk of infection to healthcare workers and reduce costs associated with sample collection. Avoidance of aerosol‐generating procedures (nasopharyngeal and oropharyngeal sampling) reduces the risk of transmission to others and "dry" collection (without the use of transport media) may reduce the complexity and therefore adequacy of sample collection whilst reducing equipment demands and costs ( WHO 2020b ). A further factor that may influence the choice of sample to use when implementing testing on a large scale and particularly to ensure willingness to participate in asymptomatic screening, is the acceptability of different sample types and collection procedures. Individual preferences for sample type may be context‐specific depending on ease of collection, speed with which results are obtained (for example, certain sample types may not be available or may perform less well with rapid tests) and discomfort associated with the procedure itself ( Zimba 2021 ). Some sample types (nasal and saliva) can be self‐collected with minimal instruction. Nasal swabs have been shown to cause less discomfort than nasopharyngeal and oropharyngeal swabs ( Frazee 2018 ). A study examining sampling preferences during screening for SARS‐CoV‐2 infection in schools demonstrated that 36% of children and their guardians agreeing to testing using saliva samples would have declined had the requirement been for nasal samples ( McLaughlin 2022 ). Target condition being diagnosed COVID‐19 is a disease caused by infection with the SARS‐CoV‐2 virus. The key target condition for this review is current SARS‐CoV‐2 infection, either symptomatic (i.e. with COVID‐19 disease) or asymptomatic, and detected using any molecular or antigen‐based test. We use an imperfect reference standard, where we consider the combined test results for two sample types in a single participant taken in the same clinical encounter as confirmation of diagnosis. A positive result for either sample type is considered to indicate the presence of SARS‐CoV‐2 infection whilst the absence of a positive test result on both sample types (i.e. both test results, negative) is assumed to indicate the absence of SARS‐CoV‐2 infection ( Appendix 1 ). We assume that false positives resulting from low‐level reactions during molecular or antigen testing, failures in sampling or laboratory protocols (e.g. mislabelling), or contamination during sampling or processing ( Mayers 2020 ) will be negligible. Similarly, we assume that the contribution of test positives from past rather than current infection will be minimal. Based on population prevalence surveys where SARS‐CoV‐2 infections are rare ( ONS 2020 ; Riley 2020 ), Dinnes and colleagues assumed an upper bound on the possible false positive rate of RT‐PCR of less than 0.077% ( Dinnes 2022 ). The false positive rate of rapid antigen tests has been estimated to be higher than RT‐PCR but still low (1.5%) ( Dinnes 2022 ). By contrast, false negative rates for RT‐PCR have been estimated to be as high as 20% to 30% in the first week after symptom onset ( Arevalo‐Rodriguez 2020 ; Kucirka 2020 ; Yang 2020 ). For antigen‐based tests, false negatives have been estimated to be as high as 40% in symptomatic individuals ( Dinnes 2022 ). This review is concerned with the difference in sensitivity caused by variation in the sample site or sample collection process. We assume that the impact of the testing method (molecular or antigen) on observed differences in sensitivity between different sample sites and collection methods should be minimal, provided the molecular or antigen testing method is the same (test type, gene targets, test positivity threshold, kit) for each sample in a pair, taken in the same clinical encounter. Index test(s) This review is concerned with the effect on accuracy of using different sample types (anatomical site and/or collection method) for the identification of current SARS‐CoV‐2 infection. We considered respiratory and nonrespiratory samples recommended by one or more of the WHO ( WHO 2019 ), Centres for Disease Control and Prevention (CDC; Centres for Disease Control 2021 ), or European Centre for Disease Prevention and Control ( ECDC 2021 ; ECDC 2022 ) that would be considered appropriate for use in ambulatory testing settings. Samples tested with either molecular or antigen‐based tests were considered for inclusion, providing a sample pair was tested using the same type of testing technology. Sample collection is noted to be one of the most critical factors affecting the performance of diagnostic tests on respiratory fluids ( WHO 2021 ). For confirmatory testing with RT‐PCR for patients meeting the case definition for suspected SARS‐CoV‐2, WHO recommends collecting nasopharyngeal and oropharyngeal samples in viral transport media (VTM), combined in the same tube to increase viral load ( WHO 2020a ). The CDC recommends collection of an upper respiratory tract (URT) specimen in VTM for confirmatory testing with Nucleic Acid Amplification Tests (NAATs). Saliva is described as having "highly variable quality" for confirmatory SARS‐CoV‐2 testing with NAATs ( Centres for Disease Control 2021 ) but is considered "an acceptable specimen type" for RT‐PCR testing when nasopharyngeal swabs cannot be collected in symptomatic patients or for repeated screening of asymptomatic individuals ( Centres for Disease Control 2021 ). The European Centre for Disease prevention and Control (ECDC) recommend upper respiratory tract (URT) swabs, aspirates or wash as the optimal sample types for detection of current infection with SARS‐CoV‐2, with saliva being noted as an "alternative specimen" to be used with assays detecting SARS‐CoV‐2 RNA only ( ECDC 2022 ). For rapid antigen detection tests (Ag‐RDT), it is noted that evidence of clinical performance is largely based on nasal, oropharyngeal or nasopharyngeal specimens. CDC and ECDC do not recommend use of saliva with Ag‐RDT tests, whilst WHO note that performance is better with URT compared to other sample types (throat wash and saliva) ( Brummer 2021 ; Centres for Disease Control 2021 ; ECDC 2022 ; WHO 2021 ). We also included sample types not currently recommended, but that might be considered appropriate for ambulatory testing settings, such as swabs of the oral cavity and gargle samples. Samples could be acquired using any method, with or without inactivation and stabilisation with transport media, and collected and tested by study participants, trained or untrained study personnel, or professionals such as healthcare workers or laboratory scientists ( Centres for Disease Control 2021 ). Anatomical sample site The main anatomical sites of viral infection may differ so that, for example, in some individuals, SARS‐CoV‐2 is more readily detected in saliva and in others the nasopharynx. Such differences might also be related to genomic variations between patients ( Ghafouri‐Fard 2020 ). The presence of virus at different anatomical sampling sites is also known to vary during the course of infection. Viral RNA levels in symptomatic infection have been shown to peak in the oropharynx and nasopharynx between four and six days post‐symptom onset ( Wolfel 2020 ) (about a week earlier than in the lower respiratory tract (LRT)) and remain detectable for a median duration of 12 to 18 days, longer with increasing disease severity ( Weiss 2020 ; Wolfel 2020 ). Viral load appears to reduce faster in URT compared to LRT samples ( Mallett 2020 ; Weiss 2020 ), in both mild and more severe infection ( Weiss 2020 ). This pattern of sample positivity is also observed in children, although the duration of viral positivity at each anatomical site is shorter ( Weiss 2020 ). The sensitivity of saliva samples compared to nasopharyngeal samples has been shown to be 100% within the first five days of symptom onset, dropping to 96.4% at 10 days ( Uwamino 2021 ). Upper Respiratory Tract (URT) samples The procedure for collecting nasopharyngeal, oropharyngeal and nasal swab samples is standardised and training or supervised instruction is recommended ( Centres for Disease Control 2021 ; ECDC 2022 ; WHO 2019 ; WHO 2020a ). Nasopharyngeal and oropharyngeal samples and oropharyngeal and nasal samples may be combined in an attempt to improve sensitivity. Nasal swabs can be taken to the depth of the nasal turbinates (nasal mid‐turbinate) or from the anterior of the nares (nasal anterior swabs). Some NAAT tests authorised by the FDA have the capability for self‐collection of specimens ( Centres for Disease Control 2021 ). Nasal mid‐turbinate and nasal anterior samples also have the advantages of being less invasive compared to nasopharyngeal and oropharyngeal swabs. Nasopharyngeal and nasal (anterior and mid‐turbinate) sampling techniques carry a risk of epistaxis, particularly for those with coagulopathy or on anticoagulation therapy ( Block‐Wheeler 2023 ; Sri 2020 ). Saliva Saliva is used widely as a diagnostic tool to detect viral infections such as dengue, Ebola, Zika, Yellow fever and recently emerged coronaviruses responsible for severe acute respiratory syndrome (SARS) and Middle East respiratory syndrome (MERS) ( Niedrig 2018 ). Saliva can be self‐collected with minimal training or supervision, and can be collected directly into a sterile container (direct sampling) although dilution may be necessary for viscous samples. Whole saliva is a heterogeneous mixture of saliva secreted in the oral cavity from various glands in addition to other components such as nasal and bronchial secretions, epithelial and immune cells from the oral mucosa and upper airways, food debris, tears, bacteria, and gingival crevicular fluid ( Miller 2010 ). Common collection methods include the passive drooling technique (allowing saliva to pool in the floor of the mouth and drain into a collection tube usually aided by a funnel device), the spitting technique (allowing saliva to pool in the floor of the mouth before spitting into a collection tube) and salivating (asking the patient to stimulate and collect saliva by chewing on a swab placed between the gum and cheek). "Deep throat" or "posterior oropharyngeal" saliva collection includes instruction to clear the throat by coughing or gargling before spitting into a collection device and may in effect combine sputum which is obtained from deep coughing and oral secretions (saliva). The composition of saliva is affected by factors such as the time of day, eating and drinking prior to sample collection and the precise collection method. For example, saliva obtained from spitting contains more bacteria compared to saliva collected using the drooling technique ( Bhattarai 2018 ). Other sample types included in this review We did not restrict inclusion of sample types to those currently recommended for use. We considered inclusion of other sample types if they had the potential to be deployed at scale in ambulatory populations. For example, gargling (undertaken by forcing the cricopharyngeal muscle to oscillate over the posterior pharyngeal wall with saline or water) and oral swabs (taken from the dorsal and ventral surfaces of the tongue and the buccal mucosa) are noninvasive and amenable to self‐collection ( Mane 2022 ; Tsang 2022 ). Gargle samples are also swab‐free and transport media‐free ( Tsang 2022 ). Sample collection method In addition to anatomical sites, variations in sample collection methods may affect accuracy. Collection of samples may be undertaken by different "operators"; for example, trained compared to untrained operators and healthcare workers (HCW) compared to self‐collected samples. Saliva and nasal samples can be self‐collected with minimal instruction and have been demonstrated to have comparable accuracy to samples collected by trained healthcare workers ( Tsang 2022 ). Other elements of the collection process may vary; for example, aspiration or washing rather than swabbing. Saliva can be collected by a variety of methods, as outlined above, and there is evidence that saliva collected with and without transport media may have comparable accuracy ( Bastos 2021 ). Clinical pathway Patients may be tested for SARS‐CoV‐2 when they present with symptoms, have had known exposure to a confirmed case, or as part of targeted screening of individuals with no known exposure to SARS‐CoV‐2 for the purpose of attendance at educational establishments or social gatherings. RT‐PCR is the primary method for detecting infection during the acute phase of the illness. The standard approach to diagnosis of SARS‐CoV‐2 infection for individuals presenting with symptoms typical of SARS‐CoV‐2 or who have had known exposure to a confirmed case is through laboratory‐based testing with RT‐PCR of swab samples taken from the URT (typically nasopharyngeal, oropharyngeal or combined nasopharyngeal/oropharyngeal). To expand testing capacity where molecular testing is unavailable or associated with long turnaround times, antigen tests on one or a combination of nasal, oropharyngeal or nasopharyngeal samples can be used to identify those who are likely to be infectious with results available in minutes. However, because of the performance characteristics of antigen tests, laboratory‐based testing with RT‐PCR may be considered necessary to confirm a positive or a negative antigen test result depending on the clinical history and epidemiological setting. Prior test(s) Signs and symptoms are used in the initial diagnosis of suspected SARS‐CoV‐2 infection and to help identify those requiring tests. A number of key symptoms have been suggested as indicators of mild‐to‐moderate COVID‐19, including cough, fever greater than 37.8 °C, headache, breathlessness, muscle pain, fatigue, and loss of sense of smell and taste ( Struyf 2022 ). However, the recently published review of signs and symptoms found good‐quality evidence of the accuracy of these symptoms alone or in combination to be lacking ( Struyf 2022 ). Typical symptom profiles may also change with the emergence of new variants ( Alford 2021 ) and as a result of vaccination ( Crozier 2021 ). Where people are asymptomatic but are undergoing testing for a specific purpose (e.g. universal testing of students as part of a risk‐reduction effort) or on the basis of epidemiological risk factors, such as exposure to someone with confirmed SARS‐CoV‐2 or following travel to more highly endemic countries, no prior tests will have been conducted. The presence of symptoms has been associated with a higher sensitivity of Ag‐RDTs ( Dinnes 2022 ), probably as a result of the presence of symptoms being associated with a higher viral load. Role of index test(s) The type of sample collected should be dictated by the manufacturer’s instructions for the test technology being used. Often, there is a choice of sample types for use with an individual test technology that is claimed to result in equivalent accuracy by manufacturers. However, the actual performance of different sample types may vary in practice, influenced by sample collection difficulty and the level of training received by sample collectors, as outlined above ( Index test(s) ). Under these circumstances, it is important to quantify and understand any variation in accuracy, to inform decisions about which sample type offers the potential for best test performance. Ultimately, when considering the clinical utility of different sampling sites and processes for use on a large scale, accuracy must be balanced against human and material resource needs (training required, time taken for procedure, need for PPE and specialised sampling equipment), supply chain issues (availability of swabs and transport media) and the acceptability of the sampling procedure to patients. Alternative test(s) The review was restricted to anatomical sample types and different methods for collecting those that were appropriate for use in ambulatory populations at the time of writing. Lower respiratory tract samples (sputum and bronchiolar lavage) and other nonrespiratory sample types (urine and faecal samples, serum, semen and tears) have not been included, as these sample types have not been considered for routine clinical use in ambulatory populations. The review was also restricted to testing technologies currently in use in ambulatory populations. This review is one of a series of reviews that cover the range of tests and clinical characteristics being considered in the management of COVID‐19 ( Dinnes 2022 ; Ebrahimzadeh 2022 ; Fox 2022 ; Struyf 2022 ). The findings of this review are relevant to reviews concerned with laboratory‐based molecular and antigen tests and rapid antigen tests. Rationale Estimates of accuracy from this review will help when making choices about specimen types and collection processes to support effective screening and diagnostic interventions for SARS‐CoV‐2 infection and disease. Objectives To compare the effect of sample site and collection procedure on the sensitivity of molecular or antigen tests in ambulatory populations for the detection of current SARS‐CoV‐2. Secondary objectives Where data were available, we aimed to investigate potential sources of heterogeneity according to population characteristics (healthcare setting, age, symptom status); index test (index sample) characteristics (time of test use post‐symptom onset or post‐contact with a confirmed case; experience and training of personnel collecting samples; sample collection method) and study design characteristics (use of the same COVID‐19 test kit or in house laboratory procedure for both samples in a pair). Methods Criteria for considering studies for this review Types of studies We included studies that compared two or more anatomical sampling sites, or two or more sample collection methods from the same anatomical site, from the same participant (within person) using the same type of test technology and from which a 2 x 2 contingency table comparing positive results from each sampling method could be constructed, including: single‐group studies recruiting participants before disease status has been ascertained; and studies based on either patients or samples. The method for deriving the sensitivity difference from a 2 x 2 contingency table is provided in Appendix 1 and described below under 'Target condition being diagnosed'. We excluded studies from which 2 x 2 tables could not be derived and studies where recruited individuals were preselected on the basis of testing positive on one of the sample sites being compared (second sampling in known cases). We excluded studies with fewer than 10 samples or participants on the basis that small studies are likely to give unreliable estimates of accuracy. We excluded case‐control studies that recruited known cases of COVID‐19 and, separately, participants known not to have COVID‐19. We included studies reported in published journal papers and as preprints. Participants We included studies recruiting symptomatic people presenting with a suspicion of current SARS‐CoV‐2 infection and asymptomatic people being tested for infection (close contacts of known SARS‐CoV‐2 infection, community‐based testing programmes including contact tracing and asymptomatic screening). We excluded studies undertaking repeated testing for the purposes of documenting viral shedding. Index tests We included upper respiratory tract (URT) samples, saliva samples, oral samples and gargle samples. We included samples acquired and tested by study participants, trained or untrained study personnel, or professionals such as healthcare workers or laboratory scientists, using any collection method, with or without inactivation and stabilisation with transport medium, using any molecular or antigen‐based testing method. We excluded lower respiratory and other non‐respiratory samples such as urine, faeces, blood, tears and semen as not suitable for testing in an ambulatory setting. For the purposes of this review, a sample pair is defined as two samples collected from the same participant tested with the same test technology within the same clinical encounter. Sample pair comparisons encompass: two samples, one collected from the nasopharynx or the naso/oropharynx and combined in the same sample container, and one collected from a different anatomical site; and two samples from the same anatomical site collected by personnel with different levels of training or supervision (for example, healthcare worker (HCW) versus self‐collection). Within a sample pair, we defined a reference sample and an index sample collected from the same participant within the same clinical encounter. Where the sample comparison was different anatomical sites, the reference standard was defined as a nasopharyngeal or combined naso/oropharyngeal sample collected into the same sample container and the index sample as the alternative anatomical site. Where the sample comparison was concerned with differences in sample collection method from the same site, we defined the reference sample as that closest to standard practice for that sample type (for example, nasopharyngeal swab rather than nasopharyngeal aspirate). Where the sample pair comparison was concerned with differences in personnel collecting the sample, the more skilled or experienced operator was considered the reference sample. Target conditions The target condition was current SARS‐CoV‐2 infection (either symptomatic or asymptomatic). Reference standards In this review, the combined test results of two different samples being compared (index and reference samples) in the same participant with the same molecular or antigen test constituted the reference standard. The absence of a positive test result on two or more different sample types taken in the same clinical encounter in the same participant was assumed to indicate an absence of SARS‐CoV‐2 infection. The analytical approach to this review precluded estimation of specificity. We assumed that the impact of false negatives and false positives on estimates of the difference in sensitivity for different sample types should be minimal, provided the molecular or antigen testing method was the same (test type, gene targets, test positivity threshold, kit manufacturer) for each sample in a pair, taken in the same clinical encounter. Search methods for identification of studies Due to the living nature of this Cochrane series of reviews, the sources used for searching changed over time. We used two main sources for our electronic searches. These strategies were devised with the help of an experienced Cochrane Information Specialist with broad diagnostic test accuracy review expertise (RSp). Searches aimed to identify all articles related to COVID‐19 and SARS‐CoV‐2 and were not restricted to those evaluating a particular type of test. The searches, therefore, did not use terms specifically focused on an index test, diagnostic accuracy or study methodology, to provide information to several reviews belonging to this series simultaneously ( Dinnes 2022 ; Fox 2022 ; Struyf 2022 ). Electronic searches Cochrane COVID‐19 Study Register searches We used the Cochrane COVID‐19 Study Register ( covid-19.cochrane.org ) for searches conducted from the inception of the register to 28 March 2020. At that time, the register was populated by searches of PubMed, as well as trials registers at US National Institutes of Health Ongoing Trials Register ClinicalTrials.gov ( clinicaltrials.gov ) and the WHO International Clinical Trials Registry Platform ( apps.who.int/trialsearch ). Search strategies were designed for maximum sensitivity to retrieve all human studies on COVID‐19 and SARS‐CoV‐2 with no language limits ( Appendix 2 ). To ensure comprehensive coverage, we also downloaded records from the 'Bern feed' from 1 January to 28 March 2020 and de‐duplicated them against those obtained via the Cochrane COVID‐19 Study Register. We decided to continue with the Bern feed given the enormous number of COVID‐19 studies available only as pre‐prints at the time. COVID‐19 Living Evidence Database from the University of Bern From 28 March 2020 to 17 February 2022, we used the COVID‐19 Open Access Project living evidence database (COAP) from the Institute of Social and Preventive Medicine (ISPM) at the University of Bern ( COVID‐19 Open Access Project (COAP) 2020 ). The database was constructed from daily (Monday to Friday) systematic searches of Embase via OVID, MEDLINE via PubMed, bioRxiv and medRxiv. The strategies as described on the COAP website are reported in Appendix 3 . Due to the increased volume of published and pre‐print articles, from 25 May 2020 onwards, we used artificial intelligence text analysis to conduct an initial classification of documents, based on their title and abstract information, for relevant and irrelevant documents ( Appendix 4 ). Other electronic sources Before 28 March 2020 (when we began using the "Bern feed"), we identified Embase records through CDC, Stephen B Thacker CDC Library, COVID‐19 Research Articles Downloadable Database ( cdc.gov/library/researchguides/2019novelcoronavirus/researcharticles.html ). We de‐duplicated them against results from the Cochrane COVID‐19 Study Register ( Appendix 2 ). We also checked our search results against two additional repositories of COVID‐19 publications up to 30 September 2020: Evidence for Policy and Practice Information and Co‐ordinating Centre (EPPI‐Centre) "COVID‐19: Living map of the evidence" ( eppi.ioe.ac.uk/COVID19_MAP/covid_map_v4.html ); and Norwegian Institute of Public Health "NIPH systematic and living map on COVID‐19 evidence" ( www.nornesk.no/forskningskart/NIPH_diagnosisMap.html ). Both repositories allow their contents to be filtered according to studies potentially relating to diagnosis. Searching other resources We contacted or accessed the websites of independent research groups undertaking test evaluations, including studies co‐ordinated by FIND ( finddx.org/covid-19/sarscov2-eval ) and the Diagnostics Global Health listing of manufacturer‐independent evaluations of antigen detecting rapid diagnostic tests (Ag‐RDTs) for SARS‐CoV‐2 ( diagnosticsglobalhealth.org ). Data collection and analysis Selection of studies A team of experienced systematic review authors from the University of Birmingham screened the titles and abstracts of all records retrieved from the literature searches. Two review authors (CD, IA, MM‐H, AC, DB‐G) independently screened studies in Covidence . A third, senior review author resolved any disagreements (CD, IA). We tagged all records selected as potentially eligible according to the Cochrane COVID‐19 diagnostic test accuracy review(s) for which they might be eligible, and we then exported them to separate Covidence reviews for each review title. We obtained the full texts for all studies flagged as potentially eligible. Two review authors independently screened the full texts for one of the COVID‐19 biomarker reviews (molecular, antigen, antibody tests or sampling). We resolved any disagreements about study inclusion through discussion with a third review author. Up to September 2020, screening was conducted across all Cochrane COVID‐19 DTA biomarker reviews (molecular, antigen, antibody tests or sampling), using tagging of records according to the review(s) for which they might be eligible. From September 2020 onwards, review‐specific searches were implemented such that screening was conducted without the requirement for study tagging for different reviews. Data extraction and management One review author extracted the characteristics of each study, which a second review author checked (CD, MM‐H, IA, AC, DB‐G). Two review authors independently performed data extraction of 2 x 2 contingency tables of positive and negative results by sample type ( Appendix 1 ). Disagreements were resolved by discussion. Where possible, we separately extracted data according to setting, age, symptom status, time post‐symptom onset or post‐contact with a confirmed case, training of the person collecting the index test sample, use of transport medium and whether identical manufacturer testing kits or in‐house laboratory testing procedures were used for each sample in a pair. Where there was uncertainty about the eligibility of a study or where studies were considered eligible, but we were not able to extract 2 x 2 contingency tables, we attempted to contact authors for the required information. A total of five authors were successfully contacted for clarification about inclusion decisions. Assessment of methodological quality Two review authors independently assessed the risk of bias and applicability concerns using the QUADAS‐2 ( Whiting 2011 ) and QUADAS‐C ( Yang 2021 ) checklists, tailored to this review ( Appendix 5 ) (CD, MM‐H, IA, AC, DB‐G). Disagreements were resolved by discussion. In assessing the risk of bias in included studies, we considered methods for participant selection into studies (participant selection domain), methods for comparing each index and reference sample pair in a study (index test domain) and the flow of participants through a study (flow and timing domain). For this review, the combined positive results of index and reference samples were used as a proxy for the number of cases of SARS‐CoV‐2 in a study population to allow estimation of the sensitivity of each sample type in a pair. As part of tailoring of QUADAS‐2 for this review, we therefore did not use the reference standard domain and instead added questions to the index test domain to assess the risk of bias for the index and reference sample pair comparison. In assessing the applicability of study findings, we considered whether study participants were representative of individuals at the point of testing to make a diagnosis of SARS‐CoV‐2 (in any setting), that testing was done with available technology, and the sampling process was described in sufficient detail to be replicable. For participant selection, we considered that, ideally, studies examining the accuracy of different sampling techniques for the diagnosis of SARS‐CoV‐2 should prospectively recruit a representative (random or consecutive) sample of participants who would undergo testing for the diagnosis of SARS‐CoV‐2 in practice (intended use setting). We excluded diagnostic case‐control studies recruiting people with and without the target condition, as these studies are known to overestimate test accuracy ( Rutjes 2006 ). Individuals should not be excluded from a study population because they are difficult to diagnose or because they have difficulty complying with a sample technique. Similarly, study populations should not be enriched with individuals who are less likely (convenience sample with other disease) or more likely (having recently received a previous positive SARS‐CoV‐2 test result) to have the target condition. To be certain that any observed differences in accuracy between a sample pair were due to the sampling site or procedure, all other elements of the testing process should be comparable. The order in which certain sample types are collected may be important to avoid contamination (for example, for a comparison between nasal and nasopharyngeal sites or between oropharyngeal and nasopharyngeal sites). Similarly, although recent research indicates that repeated sampling of the same sample site does not reduce SARS‐CoV‐2 test performance ( Levy 2021 ), care should be taken if there are implications from learning effects for comparisons of different collection procedures from the same sample site. These effects can be mitigated using random ordering of sample collection or sampling from opposite nares for nasopharyngeal and nasal sample types. Factors aside from the sample site and sampling procedure that could impact on accuracy (specimen storage and transport including use of transport medium, extraction and testing kits, gene targets and test positivity threshold) should be detailed. Test results (presence or absence of SARS‐CoV‐2) from comparison sample sites or sample collection methods should be interpreted blind to each other. Studies should report data for all study participants, including those where the sample taken was inadequate, the SARS‐CoV‐2 test was invalid, or the test result was indeterminate, to allow assessment of differences in the proportions and reasons for missing data between sample sites or sample procedures being compared. Studies should report whether results relate to participants (one sample per participant), or samples (multiple samples per participant). For assessment of applicability, the study setting is an indicator of the spectrum and prevalence of disease. Setting is also a proxy for other elements of the sampling and testing process that may have an impact on test accuracy, such as operator experience and skill and practical challenges associated with taking and processing samples. Studies should detail the setting in which testing is taking place (for example, community, primary care, dedicated COVID‐19 testing facility, hospital outpatient or inpatient). The symptom status of participants should be documented, as well as time since symptom onset and, if relevant, exposure history (time post‐contact with a confirmed case of SARS‐CoV‐2). Studies on asymptomatic people at risk of infection should document the time of exposure or, where tests are being applied for screening purposes, the indication for screening should be provided (for example, targeted screening in educational settings). Statistical analysis and data synthesis We assumed that the false positive rate from molecular and antigen tests would be low for all sample collection methods. Further, we assumed that for each sample pair, tested under the same laboratory conditions (extraction, molecular or antigen testing kit or in‐house laboratory procedure, gene targets and thresholds), that any differences in sensitivity between sample types, not driven by the sampling process itself, would be negligible. The combined results of a SARS‐CoV‐2 test (molecular or antigen tests) on two or more different sample sites constituted the reference standard. We estimated the sensitivity of each index sample site (nasopharyngeal/oropharyngeal collection combined in the same sample container, nasopharyngeal alone, oropharyngeal alone, oropharyngeal/nasal samples combined in the same sample container, nasal, saliva, oral, gargle) or the person collecting the sample (self‐collection, supervised self‐collection, healthcare professional (HCW)) in a pair, as the number of test positives from that sample site/sample collection operator divided by the total number of test positives (positive on either sample in a pair). Where indeterminate results were reported, these were classed as positive for the purposes of the primary analyses, reflecting the fact that indeterminate results are more aligned to a positive rather than a negative test result in terms of clinical actions. We present estimates of the difference in the sensitivity (reference sample (%) minus index sample sensitivity (%)) in a pair and as an average across studies for each index sampling method using forest plots and tables. If the reported difference in sensitivity is negative, the index sample misses more cases of SARS‐CoV‐2 infection compared to a nasopharyngeal sample. If the difference in sensitivity is positive, more cases of SARS‐CoV‐2 infection (true positives (TP)) are detected by the index sample compared to the nasopharyngeal sample. We expressed the difference in sensitivity % in percentage points such that, for example, a reference sample sensitivity of 98% compared to an index sample sensitivity of 96% would be presented as "‐2 percentage points.” As heterogeneity is apparent in many analyses, these summary estimates must be interpreted as the average of a distribution of values. We did not make any formal comparisons between the sensitivity of index sampling sites (nasopharyngeal, oropharyngeal, oropharyngeal/nasal, nasal, saliva, oral, gargle) or sample collection operator (self‐collection, supervised self‐collection, healthcare professional) because of heterogeneity in study participants, index sample type, collection procedures and reference sample types used. We obtained the pooled sensitivity difference and its 95% confidence intervals using the inverse variance random‐effects approach ( DerSimonian 1986 ). Statistical heterogeneity was measured using the between‐study variance, tau 2 (τ2) from the random‐effects analyses ( Rucker 2008 ). In contrast to I 2 (the percentage of variability due to heterogeneity between studies rather than sampling error), τ2 is a measure of the underlying between‐study variance. Unlike I 2 , therefore, τ2 is not dependent on the size of the included studies, and does not tend to 1, as sampling error tends to 0 when included studies are large. The square root of τ2, τ, is measured in the same units as a study outcome and thus τ2 can be directly used to quantify variability. In a review, we can therefore comment on the relative heterogeneity of one meta‐analysis compared to another measuring the same outcome. When the within‐study variance of the sensitivity difference equals zero, it leads to the exclusion of the study from the calculation of the pooled estimates, potentially introducing bias. Therefore, a correction is applied to this zero variance, allowing those studies to be included in the pooled estimates. Further details on the data synthesis techniques are given in Appendix 1 . All statistical analyses were performed using Stata/SE 17.0 ( STATA ). Investigations of heterogeneity We examined heterogeneity between studies by visually inspecting the forest plots for the difference in sensitivity. Where adequate data were available within anatomical sample sites (more than three studies per subgroup), we used univariable random‐effects meta‐regression to statistically compare sensitivity differences between subgroups according to the following characteristics. We performed a sensitivity analysis whereby we calculated pooled estimates without the zero variance correction, therefore excluding studies with a within‐study variance of the sensitivity difference of zero. We then compared results between the main analysis with the correction applied and the sensitivity analysis without the correction. We also undertook sensitivity analysis to investigate the effect of using different manufacturer kits or in‐house laboratory procedures on the same SARS‐CoV‐2 test technology for different samples in a pair. Results were compared with the main analysis (evaluations irrespective of whether the same test kit had been used or in‐house laboratory procedures followed) and the sensitivity analysis (eliminating studies where different kits or different in‐house laboratory procedures had been used). Assessment of reporting bias We made no formal assessment of reporting bias. Summary of findings We summarised key findings in a Table , indicating the strength of evidence for each index sample type, findings, and highlighted important gaps in the evidence. Results Results of the search We screened a total of 37,191 unique records (published or preprints). Of 1871 records selected for further assessment for inclusion in any of the four molecular, antigen or antibody test reviews, we identified 318 full‐text reports requiring assessment for inclusion in this review. See Figure for the PRISMA flow diagram of search and eligibility results. We contacted the authors of five studies (seven evaluations) for information to clarify eligibility concerning participant selection or study design. Four studies (six evaluations) were subsequently included: Desai 2021(a)[A] ; Desai 2021(a)[B] ; Desai 2021(a)[C] ; Desai 2021(b) ; Smith‐Jeffcoat 2021 ; Teo 2021 (a) ; Teo 2021 (b) ; Walker 2021 and one study (one evaluation) was excluded because the study population was pre‐selected ( Zobrist 2022 ). 1 PRISMA flow diagram We included 106 reports in this review, and we excluded 212 that did not meet our inclusion criteria. Exclusions were mainly because study populations were pre‐selected, i.e. samples were obtained from previously confirmed cases rather than for the primary diagnosis of SARS‐CoV‐2 (n = 79), because paired samples were not used (n = 49), or because of an ineligible study design (healthy controls or multiple samples per patient (n = 43)). The reasons for exclusion of all 211 publications are provided in Excluded studies . Of the 106 study reports, seven were only available as preprints at the time of writing ( AbdulRahman 2020a ; Becker 2020 ; Bikos 2021 ; Da Silva 2022 ; Fernández‐Pittol 2020 ; Marx 2021 (a) ; Miller 2020 ). Four study reports were independent evaluations of SARS‐CoV‐2 antigen detection rapid diagnostic (Ag‐RDT) tests made available to us by FIND, the global alliance for diagnostics ( www.finddx.org ): FIND (a) 2021 ; FIND (b) 2021 ; FIND (c) 2021(a) ; FIND(c) 2021 (b) ; FIND(s) 2021 ). For the purposes of this review, each participant contributes a sample pair (one index sample and one reference sample) and 'index tests' are the different anatomical sample sites or collection processes. The 106 included study reports related to 135 participant cohorts (a study reporting results for participants in multiple settings) and 154 separate evaluations of index tests (17 of the 135 participant cohorts evaluated two index tests and two of the 135 participant cohorts evaluated three index tests). When naming studies, we use the letters (a), (b) and (c) to indicate data from different participant cohorts in the same study report. We use the letters [A], [B] and [C], etc., in square brackets to indicate data on multiple index tests evaluated amongst the same participants. chain reaction; TMA: transcription‐mediated amplification MMost of the studies were conducted in Europe (35/106, 33%) and the USA (29/106, 27%). Nineteen (18%) studies were conducted in Asia, 15 (14%) in South America, four in Canada, two in Africa and two in Australia ( Appendix 6 ). Study design See Appendix 6 . Most evaluations were of a single‐group design, recruiting participants suspected of having SARS‐CoV‐2 infection. Four evaluations employed a two‐group design, where participants tested for suspected SARS‐CoV‐2 infection were subsequently recruited after a positive or negative reference (nasopharyngeal) sample test result and received the index sample collection within a 24‐hour period ( Guclu 2020 (a) ; Kojima 2020 ; McCormick‐Baw 2020 ; McCulloch 2020 ). Two evaluations enriched a single group of participants suspected of SARS‐CoV‐2, either with participants positive on a reference (nasopharyngeal) sample within the preceding 24 hours ( Callahan 2021(a) ), or with samples from participants on dedicated COVID‐19 inpatient wards whose disease status (suspected or confirmed positive) at the time of sampling was unclear ( McCormick‐Baw 2020 ). Most evaluations were prospective (124/154, 81%), nine (6%) were retrospective, one study employed a mixed prospective and retrospective design and in 20 (13%) evaluations this was unclear. Almost all (150/154, 97%) evaluations evaluated the effect on accuracy of different anatomical sampling sites. Of these, 130/150 (87%) used a nasopharyngeal swab and 20/150 (13%) used a combined naso/oropharyngeal swab as a reference sample site. Four evaluations assessed the difference in accuracy between operators with different levels of expertise sampling the same site. Two of these four evaluations were concerned with the effect of operator experience on the accuracy of nasopharyngeal samples ( Abdollahi 2020a ; Amoo 2021 ), one on oropharyngeal samples ( Abdollahi 2020b ), and one on saliva samples ( Kojima 2020 ). Setting for testing Some evaluations were conducted in dedicated COVID‐19 testing clinics or drive‐through venues (43/154, 28%), or in ambulatory hospital settings (38/154, 25%). Twenty‐one (14%) evaluations were recruited from community settings (primary care, participant homes or not otherwise specified), 20 (13%) included participants from mixed settings and, in 17 (11%), the study setting was unclear. A minority of evaluations was conducted in inpatient settings (9/154, 6%) as part of targeted screening (5/154, 3%) or contact tracing (1/154, < 1%). The preponderance of evaluations in dedicated COVID ‐19 testing sites and ambulatory settings was seen across all sample types/index tests. Missing data and indeterminate results Forty‐eight of 154 (31%) evaluations reported invalid or uninterpretable samples. Evaluations of saliva (36/90, 40%), and gargle (2/6, 33%) samples and evaluations of the effect of operator training on accuracy (1/3, 33%) contributed slightly more invalid or uninterpretable results compared to nasal samples (9/37, 24 %). For saliva, invalid samples were most often a result of inadequate volume or hyper viscosity of samples. For other sample types, the reason for invalid or uninterpretable results was not provided. Twenty‐one of 154 (14%) evaluations (13 saliva, six nasal, one oral and one evaluation evaluating the effect of operator training on accuracy) reported lost samples. Eighteen of 154 (12%) evaluations (16 saliva and two nasal) reported the occurrence of indeterminate test results. For the purposes of analysis in this review, indeterminate results were classed as positive (see Statistical analysis and data synthesis ). Participant characteristics See Appendix 6 . Participant demographics More than half of evaluations (91/154, 59%) were conducted on adults, 28/154 (18%) were conducted in mixed populations, and seven of 154 (4%) (six self‐collected saliva and one healthcare professional‐collected nasal) were conducted on children. In 28 (18%) evaluations, the age of participants was unclear. Symptoms and exposure history Just under half of the evaluation cohorts (71/154, 46%) were conducted on mixed symptomatic and asymptomatic participants, one‐third (51, 33%) on symptomatic participants, seven (5%) on asymptomatic participants and, in 25 (16%) of evaluation cohorts, symptom status was not reported. Forty of 154 evaluation cohorts (26%) reported whether participants had been exposed to a confirmed case of SARS‐CoV‐2. Of the 37/40 evaluations reporting the proportion of participants exposed, the median was 22%, ranging between 0% ( Teo 2021 (a) ) and 100% ( Boutros 2021 (b) ; Marquette 2021 (a) ; Marquette 2021 (b) ; Marquette 2021 (c) ; Teo 2021 (b) ) in contact tracing settings. Timing of testing in relation to symptom onset or contact with health services In more than half of evaluations (96/154, 62%), the time of sampling in relation to symptom onset was not stated. Of the 58 evaluations with 'time of sampling post‐symptom onset' reported, 39/58 (67%) were within one week of onset, 13/58 (22%) were within two weeks and 6/58 (10%) were within three weeks. The preponderance of evaluations within one week post‐symptom onset was observed across all sample types/index tests. Index tests Index sample collection method See Appendix 6 . The level of detail provided about sample collection varied considerably across evaluations. In 62% (96/154) of evaluations, we considered sufficient detail was provided to allow replication of sample collection or a commercial kit was used ( Figure ). This varied from 100% for oropharyngeal/nasal (4/4) and oral rinse (2/2) samples, to 75% (3/4) for oral samples, 64% (58/90) for saliva samples, 57% (4/7) for evaluations evaluating the effect of operator experience, 54% (20/37) for nasal samples, and 50% for operator (2/4) and gargle (3/6) index samples. Examples of information provided by evaluations included the angle and depth to which swabs should be inserted, whether one or both nares/sides of the oropharynx should be swabbed, the number of times swabs should be rotated, whether there should be a delay between eating and drinking and saliva collection, whether collection of saliva samples should be preceded by coughing, and the volume of saliva sample required. 2 Methodologial quality graph: all sample types Most of the index samples in evaluations were either self‐collected (88/154, 57%) or self‐collected whilst supervised by a healthcare worker (HCW) (36/154, 23%). Only 18 (12%) evaluations reported sample collection by a HCW: 11/37 (30%) for nasal samples, four of seven (57%) for oropharyngeal samples, two of four (50%) mixed nasal/oropharyngeal samples, and in one of 90 (1%) saliva evaluations. In 13/154 (8%) evaluation cohorts, the person collecting the sample was not stated. In 69 of the 90 evaluations of saliva compared to nasopharyngeal or naso/orpharyngeal samples combined in the same collection container, five different collection methods were described. Where described, many (34/69, 49%) collection methods involved spitting into a collection device. Drooling, salivating and deep throat were described by 11 (16%) each, whilst combined swab and drool collection was described by one evaluation. Twenty of the 90 evaluations of saliva (22%) reported using a commercially available collection device, including Salivette tubes (SARSTEDT Ag & Co, Numbrecht, Germany) (n = 6; Aita 2020 ; Fernández‐Pittol 2020 ; Huber 2021 (a) ; Melo Costa 2021 (a); Melo Costa 2021 (b); Melo Costa 2021 (c); Vlek 2020 ; Walker 2021 ); Saliva and RNA Collection and Preservation device (Norgen Biotek, Thorold, Ontario, Canada) (n = 5; Mestdagh 2021 (a)[A] ; Mestdagh 2021 (a)[B] ; Mestdagh 2021 (c)[A] ; Mestdagh 2021 (c)[B] ; Mestdagh 2021 (d)[A] ; Mestdagh 2021 (d)[B] ; Mestdagh 2021 (e)[A] ; Mestdagh 2021 (e)[B] ; Mestdagh 2021 (f)[A] ; Mestdagh 2021 (f)[B] ); OMNIgene‐ORAL, OM‐ 505 (DNA Genotek, UK) (n = 2; Becker 2020 ; Miller 2020 ); the Orasure Oragene DX (OGD‐510 device, Canada) (n = 2; Boerger 2021 ; Hamilton 2021 ), and the Saliva collection Kit (Comedical, Trento, Italy) (n = 2; Fronza 2021 (a) ; Fronza 2021 (b) ). One evaluation each used the Spectrum DNA TM saliva collection device (Spectrum Solutios, Draper, UT) ( Bruxvoort 2021 ), the OraCollect RNA, DNA Genotek, (Kanata, Ontario, Canada) ( Mestdagh 2021 (b)[A] ; Mestdagh 2021 (b)[B] ), the DNA/RNA Shield Saliva Sputum Collection Kit eDX (Zymo Research, Irvine, CA) ( Sahajpal 2021 ), and the SDNA 1000 Saliva Collection Device (Solutions LLC, USA) ( Torres 2021 ). In 34 of the 37 (92%) evaluations of nasal samples, the precise location of collection was reported: 19/37 (51%) evaluations sampled from the mid‐turbinates and 15/37 (41%) sampled from the anterior nares. Reference sample site See Table , Table and Table . For the 151 evaluations comparing the accuracy of different anatomical sites, most (131/151, 87%) used HCW‐collected nasopharyngeal samples as the reference sample site, with the remainder (20/151, 13%) using a combined oropharyngeal /nasopharyngeal swab in the same collection container. In three of 154 evaluations, the effect of sample operator on the accuracy of samples from the same anatomical sample site was examined: HCW compared to self‐collection of oropharyngeal samples ( Abdollahi 2020a ; Abdollahi 2020b ), HCW compared to self‐collection of nasopharyngeal samples ( Amoo 2021 ), and supervised self‐collection compared to unsupervised self‐collection of saliva ( Kojima 2020 ). Index sample storage and transport See Table , Table and Table . Approximately half of samples were collected and stored in transport media (79/154, 51%). Sampling without the use of viral transport media was reported explicitly in 57/154 (37%) collections. In 50 of 57 evaluations not using transport media, the sample was collected and stored dry (43 saliva, seven nasal), and in seven the sample was collected into either water or saline (three gargle, two saliva, two oral rinse). Eighteen of 154 evaluations did not report whether viral transport media were used. Testing methods used for sample comparisons See Table , Table and Table . A majority (140/154; 91%) of evaluations used RT‐PCR to detect SARS‐CoV‐2 in study samples. Four evaluations used isothermal techniques with saliva and nasal samples ( Desai 2021(a)[A] ; Desai 2021(a)[B] ; Desai 2021(a)[C] ; Desai 2021(b) ), two evaluation cohorts used Transcription‐Mediated Amplification (TMA) with saliva samples ( Banerjee 2021 ; Migueres 2021 (a) ), and eight evaluations used Ag‐RDT tests with nasal samples ( FIND (a) 2021 ; FIND (b) 2021 ; FIND (c) 2021(a) ; FIND(c) 2021 (b) ; FIND(s) 2021 , Klein 2021 ; Labhardt 2022 ; Lindner 2021 ). In 13 of 154 (8%) evaluations (seven saliva, three nasal, two oral and one oropharyngeal), the validity of the comparison was potentially undermined because the method of RNA extraction and/or the RT‐PCR testing kit differed between index and reference sample sites ( Becker 2020 ; Bikos 2021 ; De Oliveira 2021 ; Herrera 2021 ; McLennan 2022 ; Pere 2020 ; Rajh 2021[A] ; Rajh 2021[B] ; Rajh 2021[C] ; Sahni 2021 ; Wehrhahn 2020 (2 evaluations); Williams 2020 ). Where reported, the test positivity threshold used was the same for both samples in a comparison. The test positivity threshold ranged from Ct ≤ 27.5 ( Kannian 2021 ) to Ct ≤ 50 ( Desai 2021(a)[A] ; Desai 2021(a)[B] ; Desai 2021(a)[C] ; Desmet 2020 ). See figure 6, figure 7 and figure 8 in Appendix 7 for separate summary plots by sample type. The basis for responses to individual signalling questions is detailed in the Characteristics of included studies (see Appendix 6 ). We judged only 4/154 (3%) evaluations as having low risk of bias overall ( Boutros 2021(a) ; Boutros 2021 (b) ; Lindner 2021 ; Marquette 2021 (a) ). Fifty of 154 (32%) evaluations (32 saliva, 11 nasal, two oropharyngeal, two oropharyngeal nasal and one each of gargle, oral rinse and operator) were judged to be of low applicability concern. Participant selection In three‐quarters of participant cohorts (100/135; 74%), the risk of bias was considered unclear because of poor reporting of recruitment and inclusion criteria. The risk of bias was judged as high in 15/135 (11%) of participant cohorts because of one or more of the following features: non‐consecutive or non‐random sampling (n = 9); enriching participant cohorts with reference sample positive samples prior to testing stored index samples (creating a two‐group design) (n = 4); or because of inappropriate exclusions, for example, participants who were not able to provide a sufficient volume of saliva (n = 5). We had low concerns about the applicability of participants in approximately half (63/135, 47%) of cohorts and the applicability of participants to the review question was unclear in half (68/135, 50%) of cohorts. In three of 135 cohorts, participants were considered to be of high applicability concern because of enrichment of the sample with an unknown number of reference sample (nasopharyngeal) positives ( Callahan 2021(e) ; Wehrhahn 2020 ) or selective sampling from a primary care referred suspected sample ( Miller 2020 ). Index test In many (119/154; 77%) evaluations, the risk of bias in the index test domain was considered unclear. Twenty‐four of 154 (16%) evaluations were considered to be at high risk of bias in the index test domain because of one or more of the following features: lack of blinding between index and reference samples (n = 3), the use of different SARS‐CoV‐2 testing kits (n = 6), or because the ordering of collection of samples was likely to influence the accuracy of the index sample test result; for example, nasal samples being collected after nasopharyngeal samples in the same nostril (n = 11). For many evaluations, concerns about the applicability of the index test domain were low (94/154, 61%). Fifty‐eight of 154 (38%) evaluations were considered to be at unclear applicability concern, whilst no evaluations were considered to have high applicability concern. Flow and timing Poor reporting precluded judgements about risk of bias for participant flow and timing in many (80/135, 59%) participant cohorts. In particular, there was a lack of detail about participant flow; for example, using a Standards for Reporting Diagnostic Accuracy Studies (STARD)‐style participant flow diagram. Forty‐six of 135 (34%) participant cohorts were at high risk of bias because of one or more of the following features: the proportion and reasons for missing test results being different across index and reference samples being compared (n = 31), not all tested participants being included in the analysis (n = 12), or participants not receiving all index samples where participants received index tests at multiple time points (n = 12). Only nine of 135 participant cohorts were considered to be at low risk of bias in the participant flow and timing domain. Findings Key findings can be found in the Table . Overall, a total of 60,523 sample pairs contributed to 154 evaluations. A total of 40,342 sample pairs contributed to the 90 saliva evaluations; 12,979 sample pairs contributed to the 37 nasal evaluations; 2522 sample pairs contributed to the seven oropharyngeal evaluations; 2138 sample pairs contributed to the six gargle evaluations; 701 sample pairs contributed to the four combined nasal/oropharyngeal evaluations; 360 sample pairs contributed to the four evaluations assessing the effect of operator experience on the accuracy of nasopharyngeal, oropharyngeal or saliva sample collection; 238 sample pairs contributed to the two oral rinse evaluations; and 1242 sample pairs contributed to the four oral swab evaluations. See Table . The median number of participants contributing a sample pair across the 154 evaluations was 200 (interquartile range (IQR) 94 to 400) and the median number of SARS‐CoV‐2 confirmed samples per evaluation was 46 (IQR 25 to 77). The median prevalence (defined as a positive test result on any one sample in a sample pair comparison) across all evaluations was 23% (IQR 13% to 40%). Median prevalence was lowest in oral swab evaluations (14%), 18% in nasal evaluations, 23% in combined oropharyngeal/nasal evaluations, 25% in gargle evaluations, 26% in oral rinse evaluations, 28% in saliva evaluations, and 37% in oropharyngeal evaluations. The difference in median prevalence across evaluations is not obviously explained by differences in the distribution of setting across index test evaluations. See Table , Table and Table . The index sample is the sample under evaluation; one of saliva, nasal, oropharyngeal, nasal/oropharyngeal, gargle or oral. The reference sample is a nasopharyngeal sample in 134/154 (87%) evaluation cohorts and a combined oropharyngeal/nasopharyngeal sample in 20 (13%) evaluation cohorts. For ease, we refer to the reference sample as a "nasopharyngeal" sample (see: Table ; Table ; Table ). If the reported difference in sensitivity is negative, the index sample misses more cases of SARS‐CoV‐2 infection compared to a nasopharyngeal sample. If the difference in sensitivity is positive, more cases of SARS‐CoV‐2 infection (true positives (TP)) are detected by the index sample compared to the nasopharyngeal sample. Indeterminate results were classified as positive for the purposes of our analysis. Indeterminate results were reported for 13 of 154 (8%) evaluations. Most (9/13, 69%) evaluations reporting indeterminate results were in saliva samples (proportion indeterminate index sample results < 1% ( Herrera 2021 ) to 9.4% ( Becker 2020 )), two were in gargle samples (< 1% ( Fernandez‐Gonzalez 2021 (c) ) to 2.7% ( Dumaresq 2021 )) and one each in oral samples (1.3%; Goncalves 2021 ) and nasal samples (2.5%; McCulloch 2020 ). Sensitivity of sample types across different SARS‐CoV‐2 test technologies See Table . The included studies used a variety of CoV‐2 test technologies. RT‐PCR was used for most (140/154, 91%) evaluations. The remaining evaluations used: isothermal techniques (2/90, 2% of saliva sample evaluations and 2/37, 5% nasal sample evaluations); transcription‐mediated amplification (TMA) (2/90, 2% of saliva sample evaluations) or AG‐RDTs (8/37, 22% of nasal sample evaluations). Prior to investigating the accuracy of different sample types and variation in operator expertise combining studies that used different testing technologies, it was necessary to investigate whether performance of different sample types varied across different types of molecular test (RT‐PCR, TMA and isothermal tests). There was no evidence that the sensitivity of saliva samples (compared to a nasopharyngeal sample) varied across the three subgroups of molecular testing technologies: RT‐PCR, isothermal tests or TMA (see Table ; figure 12, figure 13 and figure 14 in Appendix 8 ). Due to the small number of evaluations and lack of evidence for a difference in sensitivity in alternatives to RT‐PCR in the saliva evaluations, we did not differentiate between test technology for investigations of heterogeneity in the saliva group of studies. Within the nasal group of evaluations (mid‐turbinate and anterior collection methods combined), there was no evidence that the sensitivity of nasal samples (compared to a nasopharyngeal sample) differed when used with RT‐PCR or with isothermal tests. Eight nasal evaluations (four with mid‐turbinate and two with anterior collection) contributed to the Ag‐RDT analysis. There was borderline evidence that the sensitivity of nasal samples (compared to nasopharyngeal samples) was different in AG‐RDTs compared to molecular testing technologies (RT‐PCR and isothermal tests); see Table and Figure . However, except for the investigation of sensitivity according to anterior and mid‐turbinate sample collection (reported below), data were too sparse to undertake the majority of investigations of heterogeneity in the nasal sample AG‐RDT subgroup (see Appendix 9 ).
