Oral swab samples (sensitivity difference ‐33 percentage points, 95% CI ‐62 to –5; based on four evaluations, 1243 sample pairs including 257 with confirmed SARS‐CoV‐2); Oral rinse samples (sensitivity difference ‐20 percentage points, 95% CI ‐38 to –2; based on two evaluations, 238 sample pairs including 65 with confirmed SARS‐CoV‐2); Oropharyngeal samples (sensitivity difference ‐17 percentage points, 95% CI ‐29 to –5; based on seven evaluations, 2522 sample pairs including 511 with confirmed SARS‐CoV‐2); Saliva samples collected using spitting, drooling or salivating (sensitivity difference on average ‐12 percentage points, 95% CI ‐16 to ‐8, based on 56 evaluations, 27,253 sample pairs including 4636 with confirmed SARS‐CoV‐2). We did not find any evidence of a difference in the sensitivity of saliva collected using spitting, drooling or salivating (sensitivity difference ranges from ‐13 percentage points (spit) to –21 percentage points (salivate)); Nasal samples (mid‐turbinate, anterior nares and unclear collection method combined) (sensitivity difference ‐12 percentage points, 95% CI ‐17 to ‐7; based on 29 evaluations, 9291 sample pairs including 1485 with confirmed SARS‐CoV‐2). We did not find any evidence of a difference in sensitivity between nasal samples from these two collection sites with RT‐PCR. Sensitivity of nasal samples for the detection of SARS‐CoV‐2 infection with rapid antigen tests See Table and Figure . Compared to a nasopharyngeal sample, there was no evidence for a difference in sensitivity of nasal samples when used with AG‐RDTs (sensitivity difference 0 percentage points, 95% CI –0.02 to +0.02; based on eight evaluation cohorts, 3688 sample pairs including 535 with confirmed SARS‐CoV‐2). Compared to a nasopharyngeal sample, there was no evidence of a difference in sensitivity between nasal samples collected from the mid‐turbinates or from the anterior nares in rapid antigen tests. The effect of sample operator expertise on the sensitivity of sample types for the detection of SARS‐CoV‐2 infection See Figure . Two evaluations concerned the effect of operator expertise on the collection of nasopharyngeal samples. One evaluation demonstrated a reduction in sensitivity with self‐collection compared to healthcare worker (HCW) collection (sensitivity difference ‐33 percentage points, 95% CI ‐58 to ‐8; based on 50 sample pairs including 24 with confirmed SARS‐CoV‐2; Abdollahi 2020a ) and the other found no evidence of a difference in sensitivity with self‐collection compared to HCW collection (sensitivity difference 0 percentage points, 95% CI ‐16 to +16; based on 216 sample pairs including 42 with confirmed SARS‐CoV‐2; Amoo 2021 ). One evaluation assessed the effect of operator expertise on the collection of oropharyngeal samples and demonstrated no evidence of a difference in sensitivity with self‐collection compared to HCW collection (sensitivity difference ‐8 percentage points, 95% CI ‐19 to +35; based on 50 sample pairs including 25 with confirmed SARS‐CoV‐2; Abdollahi 2020b ). One evaluation cohort assessed the effect of operator expertise on the collection of saliva samples and demonstrated a reduction in sensitivity of self‐collection compared to supervised (by HCW) self‐collection (sensitivity difference ‐26 percentage points, 95% CI ‐45 to – 6; based on 44 sample pairs including 27 with confirmed SARS‐CoV‐2; Kojima 2020 ). Investigations of heterogeneity For gargle samples, oral rinse samples, oral swab samples, oropharyngeal and combined nasal/oropharyngeal samples and operator experience, we were not able to undertake any planned investigations of heterogeneity because of sparse data. For saliva studies, we investigated the effect of participant age, symptom status, and operator (HCW, self‐collection or supervised self‐collection) on sensitivity compared to a nasopharyngeal sample for all saliva collection methods combined and within subgroups of different saliva collection methods. Due to sparse data, we were only able to investigate the effect of the use of transport media and time of sample collection in relation to symptom onset for all saliva collection methods combined. For nasal samples, we were able to investigate the effect of symptom status, time of sample collection, use of transport media and operator expertise (HCW or self collection) on sensitivity compared to a nasopharyngeal sample for all nasal collection methods combined and in molecular and antigen tests combined. Saliva samples We observed a lower sensitivity in HCW collected compared to self‐collected (sensitivity difference ‐9 percentage points, 95% CI –13 to –6; based on 21,984 sample pairs including 5209 with confirmed SARS‐CoV‐2) and HCW‐collected compared to supervised self‐collected (sensitivity difference ‐14 percentage points, 95% CI –22 to –6; based on 17,251 sample pairs including 2028 with confirmed SARS‐CoV‐2) subgroups in the saliva group of studies. However, this result should be interpreted with caution as the single HCW‐collected saliva evaluation in this comparison is an outlier: Castelain 2021 (sensitivity difference ‐92 percentage points, 95% CI –103 to –82; based on 501 sample pairs including 26 with confirmed SARS‐CoV‐2). See Appendix 10 and Appendix 11 . We did not observe evidence of a difference in sensitivity for saliva samples (all collection methods combined or within collection method subgroups) compared to a nasopharyngeal sample beyond that expected by chance according to age (adult versus child) or symptom status (symptomatic versus asymptomatic). We did not observe evidence of a difference in sensitivity for saliva samples (all collection methods combined) by the time of post‐symptom onset (≤ 1 week post‐symptom onset, ≤ 2 weeks post‐symptom onset and ≤ 3 weeks post‐symptom onset) or use of transport medium (transport medium versus no transport medium) beyond that expected by chance. See Appendix 8 and Appendix 10 . Nasal samples We observed a reduction in sensitivity of nasal samples compared to a reference sample greater than would be expected by chance with increasing time post‐symptom onset: ≤ 1 week post‐symptom onset (‐2 percentage points, 95% CI –3 to –0.3; based on 6764 sample pairs including 1077 with confirmed SARS‐CoV‐2); ≤ 2 weeks post‐symptom onset (‐13 percentage points, 95% CI –23 to ‐2; based on 1808 sample pairs including 240 with confirmed SARS‐CoV‐2) and ≤ 3 weeks post‐symptom onset (‐46 percentage points, 95% CI –96 to –4; based on 569 sample pairs including 149 with confirmed SARS‐CoV‐2). See Appendix 8 and Appendix 11 . We did not observe evidence of a difference in sensitivity beyond that expected by chance for nasal samples in molecular and AG‐RDTs combined (all collection methods combined or within collection method subgroups (anterior and mid‐turbinate)) compared to a nasopharyngeal sample by symptom status (symptomatic versus asymptomatic), use of transport medium (transport medium versus no transport medium) or operator expertise (HCW verus self‐collection). Sensitivity analysis We undertook a sensitivity analysis comparing the main analyses (which included evaluations where the kit manufacturer or components of a testing kit differed across two samples in a pair) with analyses where these evaluations were removed (10 evaluations of saliva samples, five evaluations of nasal samples, two evaluations of oral swabs and one evaluation of gargle samples). We also undertook sensitivity analysis comparing the main analyses (corrections applied to studies with zero variance allowing those studies to be included in the pooled estimates) and analyses eliminating studies with a within‐study variance of the sensitivity difference equal to zero (10 evaluations of nasal samples, one evaluation of saliva samples, one evaluation of oropharyngeal samples, and one evaluation of gargle samples). Our conclusions were not changed by the results of the sensitivity analyses ( Appendix 12 ). Discussion This review summarises evidence from within‐person (direct) comparisons of the sensitivity of alternative sample sites (compared to nasopharyngeal samples) and the effect of operator expertise on the detection of SARS‐CoV‐2 in ambulatory populations. The results of this review are based on published journal articles or studies available as preprints from 1 January 2020 up until 22 February 2022. In addition, we also included evaluations that were available as independent, national reference laboratory publications or that were co‐ordinated and published by FIND, and journal articles that were listed on the Diagnostics Global Health website until 30 April 2021. Summary of main results We included data from 106 studies reporting 154 evaluations, with a total of 60,523 sample pairs (participants) and 11,045 participants with confirmed SARS‐CoV‐2. The key findings are presented in Table . We summarise nine key findings from this review below. 1. There is no evidence that the sensitivity of gargle samples or deep throat saliva samples differs from nasopharyngeal samples when used with RT‐PCR. There is no evidence of a difference in sensitivity of gargle samples or deep throat saliva samples compared to nasopharyngeal samples for the detection of SARS‐CoV‐2 with RT‐PCR. There is evidence from one study that saliva collected using a combination of swabbing and drooling has a comparable sensitivity to nasopharyngeal samples for the detection of SARS‐CoV‐2 with RT‐PCR. Considerable heterogeneity exists in the evidence base for gargle samples and deep throat saliva. 2. There is some evidence that combined oropharyngeal/nasal samples demonstrate a higher sensitivity than nasopharyngeal samples when used with RT‐PCR. There is some evidence that combined oropharyngeal/nasal samples demonstrate higher sensitivity (average +7% percentage points) compared to a nasopharyngeal sample. However, this finding is based on only four evaluations (701 sample pairs) and collection methods varied (for example, two of the four evaluation samples were collected by healthcare workers, one was self‐collected, and in one evaluation this was not stated). 3. Nasal (anterior nares and mid‐turbinate), saliva (spit, drool, salivate), oropharyngeal and oral samples demonstrate a reduction in sensitivity compared to nasopharyngeal samples when used with RT‐PCR. Nasal, saliva (spit or salivate or drool), oropharyngeal and oral samples demonstrate a reduction in sensitivity compared to nasopharyngeal samples in descending order from oral swabs (average of 33% percentage points lower), oral rinse samples (20 percentage points lower), oropharyngeal samples (17 percentage points lower), saliva (spit or drool or salivate) samples (12 percentage points lower) and nasal (anterior or mid‐turbinate) samples (12 percentage points lower). Formal, indirect statistical comparison of sensitivities by sample site were not undertaken due to substantial heterogeneity and potential confounding. Overlapping 95% confidence intervals for the summary sensitivities suggest no evidence of a difference in sensitivity between these sample types, but for oral and oropharyngeal samples, the number of evaluations is small and there is substantial imprecision in estimates. 4. There is no evidence that the sensitivity of nasal samples (anterior or mid‐turbinate) differs from nasopharyngeal samples when used with Ag‐RDTs, but the applicability of this finding to self‐testing is unclear. Evidence for the accuracy of different sample types used with rapid antigen tests was limited in our review. In eight evaluations, there was no evidence of a difference in sensitivity of nasal samples compared to nasopharyngeal samples when used with rapid antigen tests. Only three of five evaluations of Ag‐RDTs documented collection methods and, in these three evaluations, the sample was interpreted by a healthcare professional or self‐collected and interpreted whilst supervised by a healthcare professional. It is therefore unclear the extent to which estimates of sample sensitivity for use with rapid antigen tests represent self‐sampling, self‐testing or healthcare worker testing. 5. There is no evidence that the sensitivity of saliva samples changes with increasing time post‐symptom onset. We did not find any evidence that the sensitivity of saliva samples differed with time post‐symptom onset, but conclusions are limited by the relatively small number of studies ≥ 3 weeks post‐symptom onset. In nasal samples, sensitivity decreased with time, from minus two percentage points at one week post‐symptom onset to ‐46 percentage points at three weeks post‐symptom onset compared to nasopharyngeal samples. The finding of a decline in sensitivity over time in nasal samples is in line with existing evidence ( Mallett 2020 ; Weiss 2020 ; Wolfel 2020 ). The lack of a decline in the sensitivity of saliva samples (all collection methods combined) over time may be a reflection of the presence of secretions from the lower respiratory tract in deep throat saliva. Viral load has been shown to decrease more slowly in the lower respiratory tract compared to the upper respiratory tract ( Mallett 2020 ; Weiss 2020 ). 6. Poor reporting hampers quality assessment. Only 3% of included evaluations were at low risk of bias overall. However, poor reporting precluded reliable quality assessment. Most evaluations were judged as having unclear risk of bias (59% in the flow and timing domain, 74% in the participant domain and 77% in the index test domain). Where risk of bias assessment was possible, methodological concerns included enrichment of cohorts with confirmed SARS‐CoV‐2‐positive participants, inappropriate exclusions (for example, because of an inability to collect sufficient sample volume), lack of blinding between samples being compared, non‐random ordering of samples being compared, and incomplete recording and/or analysis of excluded, lost or invalid samples. Similarly, poor reporting precluded assessment of applicability in the participant (77%) and index test (38%) domains. In particular, only 38% of evaluation cohorts reported time of testing with reference to symptom onset in symptomatic participants, which may confound results, particularly in index groups or subgroups containing few evaluations. The most likely impact of confounding in this review will be to undermine our assessment of the relative sensitivity of different collection methods and of different anatomical sampling sites relative to one another. 7. Poor reporting and sparse data limited investigations of heterogeneity. Age, symptom status and use of transport media do not appear to affect the sensitivity of saliva and nasal samples. We were limited by sparse data and were only able to perform some of our planned investigations of heterogeneity in saliva and nasal samples. We did not find any difference in sensitivity according to age or symptom status for any sample type, although the number of evaluations in children (saliva 6/90, 6.4%) and nasal (1/37, 2.7%), respectively, and in asymptomatic participants (saliva 6/90, 6.7%) and nasal (1/37, 2.7%), respectively, was relatively small. We did not find any evidence that the use of transport media affected the sensitivity of saliva samples or nasal samples. For nasal samples, the number of evaluations without transport media was small (7/37, 18.8%) and so the implications of this finding are unclear. However, for saliva samples, approximately half the total number of evaluations were performed without transport media (42/90, 46.7%), which increases our certainty in this finding. The effect of operator expertise on the sensitivity of samples is unclear. We only identified four evaluations that investigated the effect of operator expertise on the sensitivity of samples, and our ability to investigate operator expertise as a source of heterogeneity in this review was limited by lack of reporting and sparse data. Findings are conflicting, and where we had evidence, we found no consistent effect of operator expertise on the sensitivity of nasopharyngeal, oropharyngeal, nasal or saliva samples when used with RT‐PCR. Data were too sparse to investigate the effect of operator experience on the sensitivity of nasal samples in Ag‐RDTs. 8. Most of the evidence about alternatives to nasopharyngeal swabs has been conducted with RT‐PCR and concerns self‐sampling. Most (146, 95%) evaluations were conducted with molecular tests and, of these, 140 (91%) were conducted with RT‐PCR. Only eight evaluations using nasal samples were conducted with Ag‐RDTs. Many of the index samples used for molecular tests were self‐collected (57%) or self‐collected whilst supervised by a healthcare professional (23%). Most of the evaluations of samples for use with RT‐PCR in this review, therefore, relate to self‐sampling. 9. Evidence about the sensitivity of different sample types is lacking in children and in asymptomatic populations. Median SARS‐CoV‐2 prevalence across evaluation cohorts was 23%. Twenty‐eight of 154 evaluations were conducted in mixed populations but only seven (5%) evaluations were conducted on children. This is particularly important given that most of the samples in this review were self‐collected. The accuracy of samples reported in this review may not be replicable in children. Many evaluations were conducted in dedicated COVID‐19 testing clinics or in ambulatory hospital settings (55%). Testing in the context of targeted screening or contact tracing accounted for only 4% of evaluations. This is reflected by the fact that 46% of evaluations were conducted in mixed symptomatic and asymptomatic populations, whilst only seven (5%) were conducted in asymptomatic populations. We were not able to demonstrate any effect of symptom status on the sensitivity of different sample types in this review, which may point to our findings being applicable in symptomatic and asymptomatic populations. Alternatively, the lack of an effect of symptom status in this body of evidence may be an artefact as a result of the relatively low number of asymptomatic evaluation cohorts contributing to this subgroup analysis. Strengths and weaknesses of the review To our knowledge, this is the most up‐to‐date and comprehensive summary of the evidence for the sensitivity of different sample sites and collection processes for the detection of SARS‐CoV‐2, based on within‐person (direct) comparisons. Our review results have increased certainty in, and are broadly consistent with, existing systematic reviews with respect to nasal/oropharyngeal ( Lee 2021 ), deep throat saliva ( Butler‐Laporte 2021 ) and gargle ( Tsang 2022 ) achieving the highest sensitivities compared to nasopharyngeal samples. Oropharyngeal, undifferentiated saliva and undifferentiated nasal sample sensitivities were between 12 and 18 percentage points lower than nasopharyngeal samples when used with RT‐PCR ( Atieh 2021 ; Bastos 2021 ; Butler‐Laporte 2021 ; Kivela 2021 ; Lee 2021 ). In addition, this review has been able to examine the sensitivity of alternative nasal (anterior nares and mid‐turbinate) samples and saliva (salivate, swab and drool) collection techniques, the sensitivity of oral samples and the effect of operator expertise on sensitivity. Due to a larger body of evidence, compared to previous reviews, we have been able to investigate the effect of symptom status, age, use of transport media and time post‐symptom onset on the sensitivity of nasal and saliva sample types. This review also presents within‐person evidence for the sensitivity difference of nasal compared to nasopharyngeal samples for use with Ag‐RDTs. Our review used a broad search, screening all articles concerning COVID‐19 or SARS‐CoV‐2. We undertook all screening and eligibility assessments, QUADAS‐2 ( Whiting 2011 ) and QUADAS‐C ( Yang 2021 ) assessments, and data extraction of study findings independently and in duplicate. Although it is possible that the use of artificial intelligence text analysis to identify studies most relevant to diagnostic questions may have led to some eligible studies being missed, we believe that the multi‐stranded search strategy used will have identified most, if not all, relevant literature. We have reasonable confidence in the completeness and accuracy of the findings up until the search date. The robustness of our findings depends on the quality of the sample pair comparisons. To this end, we restricted inclusion to within‐person comparison of sample pairs in participants suspected of having SARS‐CoV‐2 infection at the time of testing, with both sample types included in the comparison. We excluded studies where participants were exclusively preselected for inclusion based on being known as SARS‐CoV‐2‐positive in the reference sample. We further restricted studies to those where the samples being compared were collected within the same clinical encounter, excluding studies where time between collection of different sample types was reported as being longer than 24 hours. We undertook quality assessment of the sample pair comparison using items from the QUADAS‐C checklist for comparative diagnostic test accuracy studies ( Yang 2021 ), interrogating included studies for comparability of the sampling process (for example, operator skill, unless this was the sampling variable being compared), extraction process, type of SARS‐CoV‐2 test, gene targets, and disease positivity threshold. We also assessed included studies for bias that may be introduced by the order in which samples were taken (for example, comparison of oropharyngeal samples with nasopharyngeal/oropharyngeal samples and nasal samples with nasopharyngeal samples). The analytical approach to this review precludes estimation of specificity. We consider that the occurrence of false positives would be negligible for molecular and antigen‐based tests ( Dinnes 2022 ) and similar between sample sites. We assume that the impact of false negatives from the testing technology (molecular or antigen in this review) on the validity of estimates of differences in sensitivity will be minimised, provided the testing method is the same for each sample in a pair and assuming that false negatives from different sample types are not independent. The validity of our estimates of the comparative sensitivity of sample pairs, therefore, depends on the assumption that differences in false negatives arise only as a result of differences in the sample type or process being investigated, rather than other elements of the sampling and testing process. In 141/154 (92%) sample pair comparisons, the same extraction and testing kits were used for each sample in a pair. For 13 sample pair comparisons (7/90 saliva samples, 3/37 nasal samples, 2/6 oral samples and 1/7 oropharyngeal samples), extraction and/or testing were undertaken using the same method but different testing kits for each sample in a pair. A sensitivity analysis in affected index tests did not demonstrate an effect of differences in the testing process on estimates of sensitivity. The main limitations of this review arise as a result of limitations in the evidence base. Poor reporting of the sampling process itself, such as the order in which samples were collected and blinding of interpretation between index and reference samples in 77% of included evaluations, undermined a comprehensive assessment of the validity of sample comparisons. Except for saliva and nasal samples, the number of studies contributing to accuracy estimates was small, reducing our confidence in the reliability of our findings and precluding planned investigations of heterogeneity in oropharyngeal, combined nasal/oropharyngeal, gargle and oral samples. The number of evaluations in Ag‐RDTs was small and was restricted to evaluations of nasal samples. Poor reporting hampered a comprehensive assessment of methodological quality and applicability and further undermined investigations of heterogeneity. In 62% of evaluations, the time of sampling in relation to symptom onset was not stated. Most of the included studies did not report the occurrence or management of indeterminate results, which precluded sensitivity analysis investigating the effect of these on estimates of accuracy or commenting on the effect of this on the clinical utility of different sample types. Our approach to analysis of studies where indeterminate results were reported was to classify these as 'positive' for estimation of sensitivity. This approach was taken because indeterminate results are more aligned to a positive rather than a negative test result in terms of clinical action and impact on the person tested, and because excludng indeterminate results would have resulted in overestimation of sensitivity. Although our inclusion criteria and (where reported) most (67%) evaluations were undertaken within one week of symptom onset, we cannot rule out the effect of confounding by time since symptom onset on our comparison of the relative accuracy of different index sample types compared to a nasopharyngeal sample. Despite the search date of this review (22 February 2022), we consider it unlikely that research conducted since the completion of searches would alter the conclusions. Applicability of findings to the review question Most (81%) studies recruited participants prospectively on the basis of a suspicion of SARS‐CoV‐2 infection. Participants were symptomatic (33%) or mixed symptomatic and asymptomatic (46%) and the median prevalence was 23% (IQR 13% to 40%). Most (69%) studies were conducted in dedicated COVID‐19 testing centres and community or outpatient settings. Less than 4% of included evaluations were conducted in the context of targeted screening (for example, in school or hospital settings) or as part of contact tracing. Our ability to explore whether the accuracy of samples varied according to symptom status was limited, but did not appear to have an effect on the sensitivity of saliva sample evaluations. The applicability of these findings to asymptomatic, screening populations is unclear. We aimed to include studies recruiting individuals early in the course of infection. Only one‐third of evaluation cohorts (58/154) reported time of testing with reference to symptom onset in symptomatic participants. However, in most of these, 58 evaluation cohorts testing, this was undertaken within one week of symptom onset (67%) and in a minority (10%), up to three weeks post‐symptom onset. Our ability to quantify any difference in sensitivity over time post‐symptom onset with different sample types was therefore limited. Existing evidence demonstrates superior test performance with upper respiratory tract samples for symptomatic participants in the first 7 to 10 days post‐symptom onset ( Dinnes 2022 ; Mallett 2020 ; Weiss 2020 ; Wolfel 2020 ), probably corresponding with higher viral loads ( Cevik 2021 ). We consider that estimates of sensitivity for the majority of (upper respiratory) sample types in this review are likely to be the most optimistic of those possible. Virus is more likely to be detected by lower respiratory tract samples and nonrespiratory tract samples after this time. The finding in this review, that the sensitivity of saliva samples (as a nonrespiratory tract sample) does not appear to decline over time, is compatible with existing research concerned with lower respiratory tract samples ( Mallett 2020 ; Weiss 2020 ). In the evaluations conducted with RT‐PCR, only seven were conducted on children and most (80%) index samples were self‐collected. In the rapid antigen evaluations, none were conducted on children and in the three where this was reported, only one was self‐collected whilst being supervised by a healthcare worker (HCW). Our findings for evaluations conducted with RT‐PCR are therefore applicable to self‐collected samples by adults. For evaluations conducted with rapid antigen tests, it is unclear the extent to which estimates represent healthcare worker testing, self‐sampling or self‐testing in adults. Authors' conclusions Implications for practice This review summarises evidence of the sensitivity of alternative anatomical sample collection sites and collection methods to healthcare worker‐collected nasopharyngeal samples for the detection of SARS‐CoV‐2. Most of the evidence is from symptomatic adults presenting to dedicated COVID‐19 testing centres. Evidence about the sensitivity of sample types in asymptomatic populations and in children is lacking. The implications of this on the applicability of our findings are unclear due to limitations in our investigations of heterogeneity. For confirmatory testing with NAATs for detection of SARS‐CoV‐2, the WHO, CDC and ECDC recommend an upper respiratory tract (URT) sample in VTM, with the WHO specifying a combined nasopharyngeal/oropharyngeal specimen ( WHO 2020b ). CDC recommend saliva as an alternative to URT samples for confirmatory testing with NAATs in symptomatic individuals only when nasopharyngeal samples cannot be collected ( Centres for Disease Control 2021 ), and ECDC recommends saliva only with assays detecting SARS‐CoV‐2 RNA ( ECDC 2021 ). There is evidence in this review to suggest that self‐collected, combined nasal/oropharyngeal, self‐collected gargle samples and self‐collected deep throat saliva have comparable sensitivity to healthcare worker‐collected nasopharyngeal samples when used with RT‐PCR. Self‐collected samples have the potential to reduce exposure of healthcare staff to infection and negate the need for Personal Protective Equipment (PPE) with associated resource savings. This review also provides evidence that direct sampling (without the use of transport media) of nasal samples and saliva samples does not result in a decrease in sensitivity. The use of deep throat saliva with RT‐PCR, therefore, has, in addition, the potential to save resources and reduce complexity when confirmatory testing is needed at scale. Further, there is evidence from this review that the sensitivity of saliva samples does not appear to decline with increasing time post‐symptom onset. This is in contrast to a decline in sensitivity with increasing time post‐symptom onset observed with nasal samples in this review, which mirrors the decline in sensitivity with increasing time post‐symptom onset observed with URT in other reviews ( Mallett 2020 ; Weiss 2020 ; Wolfel 2020 ). This may be an important consideration for choice of sample type in individuals presenting for testing later in the course of the disease. Self‐collected saliva (spit, salivate and drool), nasal (mid‐turbinate and anterior nares), oropharyngeal and oral swabs have a lower sensitivity of similar magnitude compared to nasopharyngeal samples when used with RT‐PCR. However, the volume of evidence for oropharyngeal and oral samples is relatively small and imprecise. Despite the advantages associated with self‐collected compared to healthcare‐collected samples, and for saliva and nasal samples, the advantages offered by direct sampling, the reduction in sensitivity compared to healthcare worker‐collected nasopharyngeal swabs with these sample types may not be acceptable in testing settings where the purpose of testing is confirmation of SARS‐CoV‐2 infection. For rapid antigen tests, WHO, CDC and ECDC recommend URT samples. A limited body of homogenous evidence in this review suggests that nasal samples have comparable accuracy to nasopharyngeal samples when used with rapid antigen tests. Further, we found no evidence for a difference in sensitivity of nasal mid‐turbinate and nasal anterior nares samples. This is an important finding for rapid tests as the acceptability of sample collection is likely to be an even more important factor affecting testing uptake in asymptomatic individuals in the community. However, it is unclear in this review the extent to which sensitivity estimates generated from nasal samples used with rapid antigen tests were based on self‐collection. These estimates may therefore not be replicable outside of healthcare settings. We did not find any direct, within‐person comparisons of other sample types used with rapid antigen tests. Estimates of the sensitivity of nasal samples used with rapid antigen tests from another review (not restricted to within sample comparisons) in this series suggested a similar sensitivity compared to nasopharyngeal samples ( Dinnes 2022 ). In the same review, saliva samples used with rapid antigen tests had a lower sensitivity compared to nasopharyngeal samples (‐36.8 percentage points, 95% CI ‐43.5 to ‐30.1). Where samples have comparable sensitivity and resource implications, the acceptability of the sampling process is an important consideration. Nasal samples have been shown to cause less discomfort than oropharyngeal swabs ( Frazee 2018 ), and research has shown a preference for saliva over nasal samples ( McLaughlin 2022 ). Importantly, in this review, we were not able to demonstrate a difference in sensitivity between nasal mid‐turbinate and nasal anterior nares samples, which may have implications for the acceptability of nasal samples. However, acceptability will differ in different population groups. For example, some individuals may struggle to generate a saliva sample ( Blackmore 2020 ). A recent study evaluated the ease of self‐collection of direct saliva samples for individuals presenting for SARS‐CoV‐2 testing, and although 90% of participants perceived saliva collection as simple, one‐third of participants had difficulty collecting a sufficient saliva sample volume and 26% of saliva samples required additional processing to reduce viscosity with adverse consequences for laboratory workflow ( Plantamura 2021 ). In this review, indeterminate or invalid results were reported by 40% of saliva evaluation cohorts, 33% of gargle evaluation cohorts and 24% of nasal evaluation cohorts. For saliva, invalid samples were most often a result of inadequate sample volume or because of hyper‐viscosity of samples. Implications for research Combined nasal/oropharyngeal, gargle samples and deep throat saliva show promise as superior or comparable sample types for use with RT‐PCR. More research is needed to increase certainty that these alternative samples can achieve the sensitivity required in settings where confirmation of SARS‐CoV‐2 infection (with RT‐PCR) is the goal of testing. There is a considerable body of research concerned with the sensitivity of saliva and nasal samples used with RT‐PCR in symptomatic and mixed symptom status populations. Evidence for the accuracy of other sample types for use with RT‐PCR is lacking. Further research is needed to determine whether oral and oropharyngeal samples have comparable sensitivity to samples where estimates of sensitivity are based on a larger volume of evidence: nasal (anterior and mid‐turbinate) and saliva (drool, salivate and spit) samples. The findings of this review suggest that, in contrast to upper respiratory tract samples, the sensitivity of saliva samples may not decrease as rapidly with increasing time post‐symptom onset. Viral load is likely to be higher in symptomatic populations, and it has been demonstrated that virus is cleared more rapidly from samples from children ( Weiss 2020 ). Children and asymptomatic individuals were under‐represented in this review. More research is needed to determine whether this finding in predominantly adult, symptomatic individuals is replicable in child and asymptomatic populations within different saliva collection methods and in testing technologies other than RT‐PCR. Evidence about the sensitivity of different sample types in asymptomatic populations and in children is lacking. This may be a reflection of the lack of evidence for the effect of different sample types and operator experience for the detection of SARS‐CoV‐2 with rapid antigen tests. Although there is evidence from this review that nasal (anterior or mid‐turbinate) samples have comparable sensitivity to nasopharyngeal samples with rapid antigen tests, poor reporting means it is unclear the extent to which this represents healthcare‐worker testing, self‐sampling or self‐testing. The lack of evaluations of different samples and factors that might affect the accuracy of sample collection and interpretation in testing technologies other than RT‐PCR is an important omission given the important role of rapid antigen self‐testing in pandemic and epidemic settings. Poor reporting precluded adequate quality assessment and assessment of applicability for evidence in this review; just over half (62%) of samples provided sufficient information to allow replication of sample collection. Similarly, only 31% of evaluation cohorts (48/154) reported invalid and uninterpretable results. Future within‐person evaluations should recruit a consecutive sample of participants and provide information about age, time of testing in relation to symptom onset, and exposure. Sampling (and interpretation of rapid antigen tests) procedure should be detailed, including any instruction or training of sample collectors, extraction and testing kits used, and thresholds should be documented. To minimise bias in sample comparisons, authors should carefully consider the potential for contamination of different sample types when deciding on sample order, or randomise the order of sample collection. Interpretation of test results for each sample type should be conducted blind to other sample results. Eligibility and exclusion decisions (including test failures) throughout the whole diagnostic pathway should conform to the updated Standards for Reporting of Diagnostic Accuracy (STARD) guidelines ( Bossuyt 2015 ). Search classification model Search classification model, used from 25 May 2020 We needed a more efficient approach to keep up with the rapidly increasing volume of COVID‐19 literature. A classification model for COVID‐19 diagnostic studies was built with the model‐building function within Eppi Reviewer, which uses the standard SGDClassifier in Scikit‐learn on word trigrams. As outputs, new documents receive a percentage (from the predict_proba function), where scores close to 100 indicate a high probability of belonging to the class ‘relevant document’ and scores close to 0 indicate a low probability of belonging to the class ‘relevant document’. We used three iterations of manual screening (title and abstract screening, followed by full‐text review) to build and test classifiers. The final included studies were used as relevant documents, while the remainder of the COVID‐19 studies were used as irrelevant documents. The classifier was trained on the first round of selected articles, and tested and retrained on the second round of selected articles. Testing on the second round of selected articles revealed poor positive predictive value but 100% sensitivity at a cut‐off of 10. The poor positive predictive value is mainly due to the broad scope of our topic (all diagnostic studies in COVID‐19), poor reporting in abstracts, and a small set of included documents. The model was retrained using the articles selected from the second and third rounds of screening, which added a considerable number of additional documents. This led to a large increase in positive predictive value, at the cost of a lower sensitivity, which led us to reduce the cut‐off to 5. The largest proportion of documents had a score between 0 and 5. This set did not contain any of the relevant documents. This version of the classifier with a cut‐off 5 was used in subsequent rounds and accounted for approximately 80% of the screening burden. Appendix 5. documents.title: Corticosteroids for treating sepsis in children and adults.
documents.abstract:
BACKGROUND: Sepsis occurs when an infection is complicated by organ failure. Sepsis may be complicated by impaired corticosteroid metabolism. Thus, providing corticosteroids may benefit patients. This is an update of a review originally published in 2004 and previously updated in 2010, 2015 and 2019.
OBJECTIVES: To examine the benefits and harms of corticosteroids in children and adults with sepsis.
SEARCH METHODS: We searched CENTRAL, MEDLINE, Embase, LILACS, ClinicalTrials.gov, ISRCTN and the WHO Clinical Trials Search Portal on 31 December 2023. In addition, we conducted reference checking and citation research, and contacted study authors, to identify additional studies as needed. We updated this search in December 2024, but these results have not yet been incorporated.
SELECTION CRITERIA: We included randomised controlled trials (RCTs) of corticosteroids versus placebo or usual care (antimicrobials, fluid replacement and vasopressor therapy as needed) in children and adults with sepsis. We also included RCTs of continuous infusion versus intermittent bolus of corticosteroids.
DATA COLLECTION AND ANALYSIS: We used the same methods in comparisons of corticosteroids versus placebo or usual care, and of continuous infusion versus intermittent bolus administration of corticosteroids. The primary outcome was all-cause mortality at 28 days. The most critical secondary outcomes were (i) all-cause mortality in the long term (last follow-up from 90 days to one year) and in the hospital; (ii) length of stay in the intensive care unit and in hospital; (iii) adverse effects, i.e. superinfection and muscle weakness (within 28 days). All review authors screened and selected studies for inclusion. One review author extracted data, which was checked by the others, and by the lead author of the primary study when possible. For this update, we used Covidence software for screening and selection of studies and abstraction of data by paired review authors, with discrepancies resolved by a third review author. We obtained unpublished data from the authors of some trials. We assessed the risk of bias in trials using the Cochrane risk of bias tool (RoB 1) and applied GRADE to assess the certainty of evidence. The review authors did not contribute to the assessment of eligibility or risk of bias, nor to data extraction, for the trials they had participated in.
MAIN RESULTS: We included 87 trials (24,336 participants), of which six included only children, two included children and adults, and the remaining trials included only adults. Seventeen additional trials are ongoing and will be considered in future versions of this review. We judged 25 trials as being at low risk of bias. Corticosteroids versus placebo or usual care Compared to placebo or usual care, corticosteroids probably reduce 28-day mortality (risk ratio (RR) 0.89, 95% confidence interval (CI) 0.84 to 0.95; 72 trials, 22,915 participants; moderate-certainty evidence). We downgraded the certainty of evidence for this outcome from high to moderate for inconsistency (significant heterogeneity across trial results). Corticosteroids may result in little to no difference in long-term mortality (RR 0.97, 95% CI 0.91 to 1.03; 12 trials, 8468 participants; low-certainty evidence) and probably reduce in-hospital mortality (RR 0.90, 95% CI 0.84 to 0.97; 40 trials, 17,459 participants; moderate-certainty evidence). Corticosteroids may reduce length of intensive care unit (ICU) stay for all participants (mean difference (MD) -0.86 days, 95% CI -1.67 to -0.05; 25 trials, 8069 participants; low-certainty evidence) and may reduce length of hospital stay for all participants (MD -1.09 days, 95% CI -1.85 to -0.34; 31 trials, 16,954 participants; low-certainty evidence). The evidence is uncertain about the effect of corticosteroids on the risk of muscle weakness (RR 1.09, 95% CI 0.78 to 1.53; 7 trials, 6729 participants; very low-certainty evidence). Corticosteroids may result in little to no difference in the risk of superinfection (RR 0.96, 95% CI 0.86 to 1.07; 36 trials, 7961 participants; low-certainty evidence). Continuous infusion of corticosteroids versus intermittent bolus Four trials reported data for this comparison, and the certainty of evidence for all outcomes was very low. We are uncertain about the effects of continuous infusion of corticosteroids compared with intermittent bolus administration on 28-day mortality (RR 1.03, 95% CI 0.81 to 1.32; 3 trials, 310 participants). We downgraded the certainty of evidence to very low due to high risk of bias in all except one trial and due to imprecision. Compared to bolus administration, we are uncertain of the effects of continuous infusion of corticosteroids on long-term mortality (RR 1.36, 95% CI 1.02 to 1.81; 1 trial, 70 participants; very low-certainty evidence), in-hospital mortality (RR 0.92, 95% CI 0.71 to 1.19; 3 trials, 352 participants; very low-certainty evidence), ICU length of stay amongst all participants (MD -0.56 days, 95% CI -3.44 to 2.32; 4 trials, 422 participants; very low-certainty evidence), hospital length of stay amongst all participants (MD -0.21 days, 95% CI -4.72 to 4.30; 4 trials, 422 participants; very low-certainty evidence), risk of muscle weakness (RR 0.89, 95% CI 0.13 to 5.98; 1 trial, 70 participants; very low-certainty evidence) and risk of superinfection (RR 1.12, 95% CI 0.37 to 3.33; 2 trials, 193 participants; very low-certainty evidence).
AUTHORS' CONCLUSIONS: Moderate-certainty evidence indicates that corticosteroids probably reduce 28-day, 90-day and hospital mortality amongst patients with sepsis. Corticosteroids may shorten ICU and hospital length of stay (low-certainty evidence). There may be little or no difference in the risk of superinfection. The risk of muscle weakness is uncertain. The effects of continuous versus intermittent bolus administration of corticosteroids are uncertain.

documents.title: Antibiotics for treatment of leptospirosis.
documents.abstract:
BACKGROUND: Leptospirosis is a disease transmitted from animals to humans through water, soil, or food contaminated with the urine of infected animals, caused by pathogenic Leptospira species. Antibiotics are commonly prescribed for the management of leptospirosis. Despite the widespread use of antibiotic treatment for leptospirosis, there seems to be insufficient evidence to determine its effectiveness or to recommend antibiotic use as a standard practice. This updated systematic review evaluated the available evidence regarding the use of antibiotics in treating leptospirosis, building upon a previously published Cochrane review.
OBJECTIVES: To evaluate the benefits and harms of antibiotics versus placebo, no intervention, or another antibiotic for the treatment of people with leptospirosis.
SEARCH METHODS: We identified randomised clinical trials following standard Cochrane procedures. The date of the last search was 27 March 2023.
SELECTION CRITERIA: We searched for randomised clinical trials of various designs that examined the use of antibiotics for treating leptospirosis. We did not impose any restrictions based on the age, sex, occupation, or comorbidities of the participants involved in the trials. Our search encompassed trials that evaluated antibiotics, regardless of the method of administration, dosage, and schedule, and compared them with placebo or no intervention, or compared different antibiotics. We included trials regardless of the outcomes reported.
DATA COLLECTION AND ANALYSIS: During the preparation of this review, we adhered to the Cochrane methodology and used Review Manager. The primary outcomes were all-cause mortality and serious adverse events (nosocomial infection). Our secondary outcomes were quality of life, proportion of people with adverse events considered non-serious, and days of hospitalisation. To assess the risk of bias of the included trials, we used the RoB 2 tool, and for evaluating the certainty of evidence we used GRADEpro GDT software. We presented dichotomous outcomes as risk ratios (RR) and continuous outcomes as mean differences (MD), both accompanied by their corresponding 95% confidence intervals (CI). We used the random-effects model for all our main analyses and the fixed-effect model for sensitivity analyses. For our primary outcome analyses, we included trial data from the longest follow-up period.
MAIN RESULTS: We identified nine randomised clinical trials comprising 1019 participants. Seven trials compared two intervention groups and two trials compared three intervention groups. Amongst the trials comparing antibiotics versus placebos, four trials assessed penicillin and one trial assessed doxycycline. In the trials comparing different antibiotics, one trial evaluated doxycycline versus azithromycin, one trial assessed penicillin versus doxycycline versus cefotaxime, and one trial evaluated ceftriaxone versus penicillin. One trial assessed penicillin with chloramphenicol and no intervention. Apart from two trials that recruited military personnel stationed in endemic areas or military personnel returning from training courses in endemic areas, the remaining trials recruited people from the general population presenting to the hospital with fever in an endemic area. The participants' ages in the included trials was 13 to 92 years. The treatment duration was seven days for penicillin, doxycycline, and cephalosporins; five days for chloramphenicol; and three days for azithromycin. The follow-up durations varied across trials, with three trials not specifying their follow-up periods. Three trials were excluded from quantitative synthesis; one reported zero events for a prespecified outcome, and two did not provide data for any prespecified outcomes. Antibiotics versus placebo or no intervention The evidence is very uncertain about the effect of penicillin versus placebo on all-cause mortality (RR 1.57, 95% CI 0.65 to 3.79; I2 = 8%; 3 trials, 367 participants; very low-certainty evidence). The evidence is very uncertain about the effect of penicillin or chloramphenicol versus placebo on adverse events considered non-serious (RR 1.05, 95% CI 0.35 to 3.17; I2 = 0%; 2 trials, 162 participants; very low-certainty evidence). None of the included trials assessed serious adverse events. Antibiotics versus another antibiotic The evidence is very uncertain about the effect of penicillin versus cephalosporin on all-cause mortality (RR 1.38, 95% CI 0.47 to 4.04; I2 = 0%; 2 trials, 348 participants; very low-certainty evidence), or versus doxycycline (RR 0.93, 95% CI 0.13 to 6.46; 1 trial, 168 participants; very low-certainty evidence). The evidence is very uncertain about the effect of cefotaxime versus doxycycline on all-cause mortality (RR 0.18, 95% CI 0.01 to 3.78; 1 trial, 169 participants; very low-certainty evidence). The evidence is very uncertain about the effect of penicillin versus doxycycline on serious adverse events (nosocomial infection) (RR 0.62, 95% CI 0.11 to 3.62; 1 trial, 168 participants; very low-certainty evidence) or versus cefotaxime (RR 1.01, 95% CI 0.15 to 7.02; 1 trial, 175 participants; very low-certainty evidence). The evidence is very uncertain about the effect of doxycycline versus cefotaxime on serious adverse events (nosocomial infection) (RR 1.01, 95% CI 0.15 to 7.02; 1 trial, 175 participants; very low-certainty evidence). The evidence is very uncertain about the effect of penicillin versus cefotaxime (RR 3.03, 95% CI 0.13 to 73.47; 1 trial, 175 participants; very low-certainty evidence), versus doxycycline (RR 2.80, 95% CI 0.12 to 67.66; 1 trial, 175 participants; very low-certainty evidence), or versus chloramphenicol on adverse events considered non-serious (RR 0.74, 95% CI 0.15 to 3.67; 1 trial, 52 participants; very low-certainty evidence). Funding Six of the nine trials included statements disclosing their funding/supporting sources and three trials did not mention funding source. Four of the six trials mentioning sources received funds from public or governmental sources or from international charitable sources, and the remaining two, in addition to public or governmental sources, received support in the form of trial drug supply directly from pharmaceutical companies.
AUTHORS' CONCLUSIONS: As the certainty of evidence is very low, we do not know if antibiotics provide little to no effect on all-cause mortality, serious adverse events, or adverse events considered non-serious. There is a lack of definitive rigorous data from randomised trials to support the use of antibiotics for treating leptospirosis infection, and the absence of trials reporting data on clinically relevant outcomes further adds to this limitation.

documents.title: Armed violent conflict and healthcare-seeking behavior for maternal and child health in sub-Saharan Africa: A systematic review.
documents.abstract:
BACKGROUND: Over 630 million women and children worldwide have been displaced by conflict or live dangerously close to conflict zones. While the adverse effects of physical destruction on healthcare delivery are relatively well understood, the effects on healthcare-seeking behavior remain underexplored, particularly in sub-Saharan Africa. This study aims to better understand the interconnections and knowledge gaps between exposure to armed violent conflicts and healthcare-seeking behaviors for maternal and child health in sub-Saharan Africa.
METHODS: Five key electronic databases (PubMed, Scopus, Web of Science, PsycNET, and African Journals Online) were searched for peer-reviewed publications between 2000 and 2022. The review was designed according to PRISMA-P statement and the protocol was registered with PROSPERO database. The methodological quality and risks of bias were appraised using GRADE. A data extraction instrument was modelled along the Cochrane Handbook for Systematic Reviews and the Centre for Reviews and Dissemination of Systematic Reviews.
RESULT: The search results yielded 1,148 publications. Only twenty-one studies met the eligibility criteria, reporting healthcare-seeking behaviors for maternal and child health. Of the twenty-one studies, seventeen (81.0%) reported maternal health behaviors such as antenatal care, skilled birth attendance, postnatal care services, and family planning. Nine studies (42.8%) observed behaviors for child health such as vaccination uptake, case management for pneumonia, diarrhea, malnutrition, and cough. While conflict exposure is generally associated with less favorable healthcare-seeking behaviors, some of the studies found improved health outcomes. Marital status, male partner attitudes, education, income and poverty levels were associated with healthcare-seeking behavior.
CONCLUSION: There is a need for multifaceted interventions to mitigate the impact of armed violent conflict on healthcare-seeking behavior, given its overall negative effects on child and maternal healthcare utilization. While armed violent conflict disproportionately affects children's health compared to maternal health, it is noteworthy that exposure to such conflicts may inadvertently also lead to positive outcomes.
PROSPERO REGISTRATION NUMBER: CRD42023484004.
documents.conclusions:
There is a need for multifaceted interventions to mitigate the impact of armed violent conflict on healthcare-seeking behavior, given its overall negative effects on child and maternal healthcare utilization. While armed violent conflict disproportionately affects children's health compared to maternal health, it is noteworthy that exposure to such conflicts may inadvertently also lead to positive outcomes.
PROSPERO REGISTRATION NUMBER: CRD42023484004.

Abstract Background Over 630 million women and children worldwide have been displaced by conflict or live dangerously close to conflict zones. While the adverse effects of physical destruction on healthcare delivery are relatively well understood, the effects on healthcare-seeking behavior remain underexplored, particularly in sub-Saharan Africa. This study aims to better understand the interconnections and knowledge gaps between exposure to armed violent conflicts and healthcare-seeking behaviors for maternal and child health in sub-Saharan Africa. Methods Five key electronic databases (PubMed, Scopus, Web of Science, PsycNET, and African Journals Online) were s earched for peer-reviewed publications between 2000 and 2022. The review was designed according to PRISMA-P statement and the protocol was registered with PROSPERO database. The methodological quality and risks of bias were appraised using GRADE. A data extraction instrument was modelled along the Cochrane Handbook for Systematic Reviews and the Centre for Reviews and Dissemination of Systematic Reviews. Result The search results yielded 1,148 publications. Only twenty-one studies met the eligibility criteria, reporting healthcare-seeking behaviors for maternal and child health. Of the twenty-one studies, seventeen (81.0%) reported maternal health behaviors such as antenatal care, skilled birth attendance, postnatal care services, and family planning. Nine studies (42.8%) observed behaviors for child health such as vaccination uptake, case management for pneumonia, diarrhea, malnutrition, and cough. While conflict exposure is generally associated with less favorable healthcare-seeking behaviors, some of the studies found improved health outcomes. Marital status, male partner attitudes, education, income and poverty levels were associated with healthcare-seeking behavior. Conclusion There is a need for multifaceted interventions to mitigate the impact of armed violent conflict on healthcare-seeking behavior, given its overall negative effects on child and maternal healthcare utilization. While armed violent conflict disproportionately affects children’s health compared to maternal health, it is noteworthy that exposure to such conflicts may inadvertently also lead to positive outcomes. Introduction The health status of populations, especially women and children, tends to deteriorate in countries affected by armed conflict. Exposure to armed conflict often leads to an overwhelming loss of human life, disruptions of health service delivery, infrastructure breakdown and widespread displacement [ 1 ]. A substantial portion of the world’s women and children resides in countries suffering from armed conflicts [ 2 ]. Estimates indicate that, in 2017, approximately 630 million women and children, accounting for 10% of women and 16% of children worldwide, either faced displacement due to conflict or resided dangerously close to conflicts zones [ 2 – 5 ]. The problem is particularly pronounced in sub-Saharan Africa (SSA), where armed conflicts have been more prevalent than in other regions. For example, nearly 70% of all countries in SSA have witnessed armed conflicts since 1980 [ 2 , 6 ]. The International Committee of the Red Cross (ICRC) classifies armed conflicts as non-international conflicts involving governmental and non-government forces, including insurgency, organized crime and banditry [ 7 ]. Meanwhile, the Uppsala Conflict Data Program (UCDP) sees armed conflict as a contested incompatibility related to government and/or territory, wherein the use of armed force between the military forces of two parties, with at least one being a government of a state, has resulted in at least 25 battle-related deaths each year [ 8 ]. It is widely recognized that the impact of wars extends far beyond the cease-fire [ 9 – 11 ]. However, the underlying reasons for this phenomenon are yet to be fully understood. Some adverse long-term effects can be directly attributed to the conflict itself: unexploded ordnance continues to pose a threat to lives and livelihoods even decades after a war [ 12 ], and injuries sustained during conflicts shorten lives and compromises the health of those affected [ 13 ]. Wars have health consequences beyond the physical injuries caused by violence: destruction of sanitation and energy infrastructure can lead to the spread of waterborne and respiratory diseases [ 14 ]. Reduced functioning or restricted access to health facilities may reduce vector control and contribute to the spread of mosquito-transmitted diseases such as malaria or dengue fever [ 15 , 16 ]. Refugees and internally displaced persons may inadvertently introduce diseases into other areas [ 17 , 18 ]. The destruction of hospitals and clinics, combined with the departure of health workers seeking safety for themselves and their families, further exacerbates the health challenges in conflict zones [ 19 – 23 ]. Other factors that have been associated with maternal health outcome in armed violent conflicts include miscarriages, premature deliveries, unsafe living conditions and malnutrition [ 24 ]. Beyond tangible impacts, armed violent conflicts can have intangible effects, including the normalization of violence, shifts in social norms, and the breakdown of the social order. These elements are often accompanied by increased levels of sexual violence and voluntary unprotected sex, leading to the spread of sexually transmitted diseases [ 25 ]. The trauma resulting from violence, even if not visibly apparent, is associated with both persistent mental health issues and associated physical ailments that often afflict victims throughout their lives [ 11 ]. These latter effects may cause maternal behavioral changes such as smoking or excessive alcohol consumption/addiction, which, in turn, can negatively affect child health in a variety of ways, from pregnancy to adverse effects on birth weight, child height for age, child weight for height, immunization coverage, infant and child mortality [ 26 – 32 ]. Moreover, exposure to violence may lead to fear, mistrust, and psychological trauma, creating reluctance among individuals to seek out health-services [ 33 – 35 ]. However, while the consequences of structural armed violent conflicts abound, there is a dearth of evidence on the direct relationship between health-seeking behavior on account of experience of or exposure to armed violent conflicts in the SSA. Hence, this study aims to generate new insights into the complex interplay between health decision-making or health-seeking behavior and exposure to armed violence during and after conflicts. It seeks to generate knowledge that can be used in health promotion initiatives in conflict and post-conflict societies, especially those that aim at reducing child and maternal mortality and morbidity. The specific objectives of this study are to assess the existing body of knowledge on healthcare-seeking behaviors in armed violent conflict settings, and to explore and describe the various factors influencing healthcare-seeking behaviors in regions of SSA affected by armed violent conflicts. Methods Systematic review registration and reporting The review protocol was registered in the PROSPERO database (Reg. no.: CRD42023484004) and designed in accordance with the Preferred Reporting Items for Systematic Reviews & Meta-Analyses Protocol (PRISMA) 2020 Statement [ 36 ]. As this is a systematic review of previously published studies, ethical review and informed consent are not applicable. Data sources and search strategy An interdisciplinary review team with expertise in global health, public health, public policy, epidemiology, political science and conflict studies, social science and evidence synthesis was constituted. Guided by the Population, Intervention, Comparison and Outcomes (PICO) model for systematic review [ 37 , 38 ] (see Table 1 ), the team developed a broad research question: “How does exposure to armed violent conflicts affect healthcare-seeking behaviors for maternal and child health in sub-Saharan Africa ? ” . Study eligibility Studies were included in the review according to the PICO criteria. Predefined inclusion and exclusion criteria were developed to avoid bias due to non-relevant studies (see Table 3 ). Due to the sensitivity of the topic and to avoid an irregular time frame (using month instead of year of publication), i.e., 2000 –October 2023, the study used articles published within the year 2000–2022. Also, using articles of this sensitive nature without adequate time for feedback from the scientific community and the public could be risky due to potential corrections and retrievals. Outcome of interest Since studies on healthcare-seeking behaviors encompass a diverse demographic spectrum, ranging from infants to the elderly, this study targeted parents/legal guardians (caregivers) of children under the age of five years, pregnant women, and mothers in SSA. Healthcare-seeking behavior has been defined as any action taken by individuals who perceive themselves to have a health problem or are ill, for the purpose of finding an appropriate remedy [ 40 , 41 ]. Given the broad nature of healthcare-seeking behavior, this review focuses specifically on the utilization of health services in armed conflict settings. The impacts of exposure to or experience of armed violence conflict on health-seeking behavior in SSA were classified into two broad categories. Maternal health variables include antenatal care attendance, maternal vaccination, skilled attendance at birth, and postnatal care services (e.g., utilization of family planning services). Child health variables include the uptake of childhood vaccination from routine immunization systems, and healthcare-seeking behaviors for common health problems among children under the age of five years, such as fever and diarrhea. Quality assessment of studies and risk of bias The quality of evidence in each study in the review was assessed using the Grades of Recommendation, Assessment, Development, and Evaluation Working Group [ 42 ]. The review adhered to the World Health Organization (WHO) and Cochrane Collaboration on the principles of the GRADE system for evaluating the quality of evidence for outcomes reported in systematic reviews [ 43 ]. The authors independently assessed each relevant study using the criteria from the Cochrane Collaboration and the Centre for Reviews and Dissemination (CRD) to evaluate the risk of bias and quality of evidence [ 44 ]. Interrater reliability To assess inter-rater reliability, 10 studies were randomly selected from the 1,148 articles initially identified. Each study was independently assessed using the predefined eligibility criteria, and if there was disagreement about the decision, the process was repeated. Inconsistent decisions were discussed as a group to ensure agreement among the authors. The resulting interrater reliability Kappa coefficient was K = 0.95 (where 1.0 is a perfect score), which justified the approach of the subsequent screening processes [ 45 ]. Data extraction A data extraction instrument was developed using Microsoft Excel, based on the Cochrane Handbook for Systematic Reviews and the CRD’s Guidance for Undertaking Reviews in Health Care [ 44 , 46 ]. Two algorithms were formulated. The first concerned the characteristics of the study results. It comprised key indicators such as author last name, publication year, title of publication, country of study, study design, primary and secondary outcomes, nature of armed violence conflict, study setting, gender of the targeted group, and factors associated with health-seeking behavior that were reported in the studies, especially those related to maternal and child health. The second algorithm was used to assess the quality of evidence and risk of potential biases in each study, such as study design, selection, detection, reporting, attrition, and publication bias. In addition, the assessment considered evidence related to impression, inconsistency, and indirectness in the studies. The factors influencing health-seeking behavior due to exposure to armed violent conflict identified in the studies were systematically categorized into themes. Two authors (PS and RIJ) independently extracted data from the final included studies, and populated the two designed matrices, which were then peer-reviewed in a workshop among all authors to confirm the collected data and resolve disagreements or misinterpretations. Study analysis Significant evidence relevant to the goal of the review was extracted, appraised and reported in a systematic fashion using the PRISMA-P checklist [ 47 , 48 ]. The extracted data were synthesized to answer the research question. Results Fig 1 visualizes the country-contexts of the final set of studies that met all the review criteria. Fig 1 Eligible studies by country across SSA. The included studies cover nine countries: Nigeria, Burkina Faso, DRC, Sudan, South Sudan, Somalia, Uganda, Kenya, and Burundi: All nine countries have experienced prolonged armed violent conflicts over several decades. In Somalia, since the formation of the Al Qaeda-affiliated Al-Shabaab group, at least 1,000 deaths have been reported every year [ 49 ]. Widespread conflict has resulted in the deterioration of Somalia’s public health system with over 2.6 million internally displaced persons due to the conflict and drought [ 49 , 50 ]. In eastern DRC, nearly two decades of armed conflict have severely compromised the health system, contributing to an estimated 3.9 million excess deaths [ 51 , 52 ]. Uganda is currently recovering from over 20 years of armed conflict orchestrated by the Lord’s Resistance Army, which resulted in the disruption of health services and massive population displacement estimated at 2 million [ 53 , 54 ]. Both Burundi and Uganda are recovering from atrocious civil wars that each claimed tens of thousands of lives and caused millions of people to be displaced [ 55 ]. In West African countries like Nigeria and Burkina Faso, constant conflicts due to religion, ethnicity, and political views have posed significant challenges [ 53 ]. Currently, Boko Haram operating in Nigeria is recognized as one of the most extreme terrorist groups in SSA. Since 2009, the Boko Haram insurgency has killed more than 20,000 people and displaced more than 2 million [ 56 ]. Nigeria, Somalia, the DRC, Burkina Faso, Sudan, South Sudan, and Cameroon have often experienced very high-intensity armed conflicts, while countries such as Kenya and Uganda have experienced lower-intensity conflicts. These conflicts have involved non-state actors, terrorists, bandits, and other armed groups. The complex humanitarian emergencies caused by violent armed conflict severely impact on the already fragile national and subnational health systems in many of these countries through the destruction of health facilities and the flight of trained health workers [ 57 , 58 ]. Search results The search across five databases [PubMed, Scopus, Web of Science, PsycNET, and African Journals Online (AJOL)] yielded 1,148 articles (PubMed = 596, Scopus = 218, Web of Science = 137, PsycNET = 159 and AJOL = 38), with 77 articles removed as duplicates. Therefore, 1,071 articles were then screened for eligibility based on title and abstract. A total of 1,005 articles were excluded during this screening phase for various reasons: articles not in English (n = 3), not peer-reviewed (n = 17), health-seeking behavior not the primary outcome (n = 627), not focusing on armed conflict (n = 30), not studies in SSA (n = 86), studies of sexual or domestic violence (n = 91), studies of healthcare costs (n = 10), studies on internally displaced persons or refugees (n = 44), review articles (n = 36), and finally, studies whose focus was not maternal and child health (n = 61). The remaining 66 articles underwent a full text screening. After the screening, 45 articles were excluded for the following reasons: duplicates (n = 2), non-peer-reviewed articles (n = 1), review articles (n = 8), outcome not defined (n = 2), health-seeking behavior not the primary outcome (n = 20), not focused on armed conflict (n = 3) and maternal and child health (n = 9), respectively. The final review incorporated 21 studies reporting healthcare-seeking behaviors for maternal and child health in conflict and post-conflict settings in SSA. The screening and selection process is illustrated in the PRISMA-P flow diagram of Fig 2 . Fig 2 PRISMA 2009 flow diagram [ 59 ]. A significant proportion of the eligible studies were from Nigeria (n = 8, 38.1%), Uganda (n = 3, 14.2%), and Congo (n = 3, 14.2%). All studies were peer-reviewed journal articles. Out of the total, 13 studies (61.8%) were descriptive in design, while three (14.3%) used a pre-post survey approach. 12 studies focused exclusively on maternal health issues (57.2%) and four (19.0%) involved children exclusively, while five studies reported outcomes for both children and women (23.8%). The majority of the studies (90.5%) were published within the last ten years (2012–2022), and none were randomized control trials. The characteristics of the included studies are shown in Table 4 . Missing data in the eligible studies were very minimal, hence pose no relevance to the review outcomes. Studies whose missing data are above 0.5% are excluded. Of the twenty-one included studies, seventeen (81.0%) reported healthcare-seeking behaviors for maternal health services in settings of armed violent conflict. The reported healthcare-seeking behaviors were antenatal care attendance, skilled birth attendance, postnatal care services, family planning uptake/contraceptive prevalence rate, health facility births, caesarean section rates, unmet need for family planning, and HIV/AIDS care and treatment [ 19 , 20 , 49 , 51 , 55 , 57 , 60 – 70 ]. Nine studies (42.9%) reported healthcare-seeking behaviors for child health. The child health seeking behaviors reported were vaccines uptake (measles, BCG, and DPT), and case management for pneumonia, diarrhea, malnutrition, fever, and cough [ 49 , 53 , 60 , 66 , 68 , 69 , 71 – 73 ]. Antenatal care attendance was the most common healthcare behavior observed in most of the studies (57.1%), followed by utilization of skilled birth attendants (33.3%) for maternal health, while the uptake of measles vaccination was the most common health-seeking behavior for child health.
